kept.title: Bharadvaja asks for a fourth lifetime of study
kept.story: The story goes that the sage Bharadvaja studied the Vedas for three lifetimes, and when he was old and tired, Indra offered him a fourth. He said he would use it to study again. So Indra showed him three shapes like mountains, took a handful from each and said: these handfuls are what you learned; the Vedas have no end.
kept.asana: Bharadvajasana, Intermediate series (Nadi Shodhana), straight after Bakasana A and B (no. 16 of 42 on the ashtangayoga.info list). It is not in the Primary series.
kept.source: Taittiriya Brahmana 3.10.11.3-5, trans. John Muir, Original Sanskrit Texts, Vol. 3, 2nd ed., revised and enlarged (London: Trubner, 1868), pp. 16-17 (the Sanskrit starts on p. 16, the English is on p. 17, footnote 28 explains 'three lives'). Dedication of the asana: B.K.S. Iyengar, Light on Yoga (1966), no. 112 Bharadvajasana I.
kept.evidence: I downloaded the archive.org OCR text of Muir vol. 3. The title page reads 'VOLUME THIRD ... SECOND EDITION, REVISED AND ENLARGED' (Trubner 1868). Muir gives the passage as 'Taittiriya Brahmana, iii. 10, 11, 3' and numbers the next parts 4 and 5. The English on p. 17: 'Bharadvaja lived through three lives in the state of a religious student. Indra approached him when he was lying old and decrepit, and said to him: Bharadvaja, if I give thee a fourth life, how wilt thou employ it? I will lead the life of a religious student, he replied. He (Indra) showed him three mountain-like objects, as it were unknown. From each of them he took a handful ... These are the Vedas. The Vedas are infinite. This is what thou hast studied during these three lives.' Footnote 28: 'This does not appear to mean, three lives in three different births, but a life of thrice the usual length.' FIXES: the draft's 'three mountains' is really 'three mountain-like objects', so I wrote 'three shapes like mountains'. Part 5 (Agni Savitra, he becomes immortal) is left out. SERIES: today I fetched ashtangayoga.info/ashtanga-yoga/2-serie-nadi-shodhana/, which lists Bakasana A, Bakasana B, then Bharadvajasana. Its primary series page (41 entries) has no Bharadvajasana. IYENGAR: I checked the archive.org DLI scan of Light on Yoga (in.ernet.dli.2015.462792). Entry '112. Bharadvajasana I' says 'Bharadvaja was the father of Drona ... who fought the great war described in the Mahabharata. This asana is dedicated to Bharadvaja.' The entry number 112 is confirmed.
kept.safety: Safe as retold. Indra appears as a god, not as a king. Leave out Iyengar's Drona line, because it brings in the Mahabharata war. Leave out the immortality ending too. Present the story as a legend: Muir himself says 'three lives' may mean one very long life. It makes no health claim.
kept.joke_angle: Indra took one handful from a mountain to show what Bharadvaja learned in three lifetimes. I have had twenty years on the mat. My hamstrings are still on the first handful, and they would also like a fourth lifetime.

kept.title: The tortoise who felt a mountain as a back scratch
kept.story: The story goes that gods and asuras churned the ocean for amrita, the nectar of immortality, using a mountain as the churning stick. A tortoise held the mountain on his back; in the Bhagavata Purana he is Vishnu, and the turning mountain felt like a nice back scratch. In the Mahabharata, the gods grew tired before any nectar came.
kept.asana: Kurmasana and Supta Kurmasana, Primary series (Yoga Chikitsa). They are nos. 25 and 26 on the ashtangayoga.info list, right after Bhuja Pidasana.
kept.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Astika Parva), Section 18, trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896), Project Gutenberg #15474. Srimad Bhagavatam 8.7.8 and 8.7.10, trans. A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada (BBT); this translation is under copyright, so paraphrase it. B.K.S. Iyengar, Light on Yoga (1966), no. 133 Kurmasana. Critical edition Sanskrit: Mahabharata 1.16.10 (BORI, GRETIL).
kept.evidence: Gutenberg #15474, Section XVIII: Ananta 'tore up the mountain'. Then: 'The gods then went to the king of tortoises and said to him, O Tortoise-king, thou wilt have to hold the mountain on thy back!' Later: 'Sire, we are spent up, we have no strength left to churn further. Nectar hath not yet arisen.' In the Mahabharata the tortoise is a tortoise-king, not Vishnu. The GRETIL Sanskrit (1.16.10, 'kurmarajanam akuparam') names him Akupara, the same name as the tortoise in the Markandeya story, which is a good bridge. On vedabase, SB 8.7.8 has the Lord take a huge tortoise body to lift the sunken mountain, and SB 8.7.10 says he 'accepted the rolling of the mountain as a means of scratching His body' (adi-kacchapa). SB 8.7.18 names the poison 'halahala'. The ashtangayoga.info opening-mantra page shows 'samsara-halahala-moha-santyai', so the chant link holds, but only through the Bhagavata, because the Mahabharata calls the poison Kalakuta. In the Light on Yoga DLI scan, no. 133 reads: 'amrta (nectar) with which the gods preserved their youth'. Confirmed. ALREADY POSTED? The scratchpad has only an Oct 3 'kurma' research folder, older tortoise quotes (Xunzi, Trollope) and Hidden Stories Ep.2 to Ep.4. I found no published Kurma episode, but Boonchu should confirm.
kept.safety: Retold safely. Mahabharata 18 itself describes sea animals crushed and lions and elephants burned during the churning. Leave all of that out, along with the asuras' fight over the nectar and Rahu. Use 'asuras' and avoid any 'gods vs demons' battle framing. Do not link the 'nectar of youth' to health benefits of Kurmasana: it is myth only. Paraphrase Prabhupada and do not quote him at length.
kept.joke_angle: The tortoise carried a whole mountain and felt it as a nice back scratch. I am 53. In Supta Kurmasana I carry only my own two legs, and my back calls them a mountain.

kept.title: Ask the tortoise, he is older
kept.story: The story goes that a man whose good deeds had been forgotten asked the long-lived sage Markandeya, 'Do you know me?' The sage sent him to an older owl, the owl to an older crane, the crane to an older tortoise, Akupara. The tortoise cried and remembered him: the hooves of the cows he gave away had dug the lake.
kept.asana: Kurmasana and Supta Kurmasana, Primary series. Bonus: the Sanskrit calls the crane a 'baka' (bakah, Mbh 3.191.9), so Bakasana A and B (Intermediate series) is a direct name link. The owl has no series asana.
kept.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Markandeya-Samasya Parva), Section 198 (misprinted 'CLXLVIII' in the Gutenberg edition), trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896), Project Gutenberg #15474. Critical edition Sanskrit: Mahabharata 3.191.4-21 (BORI, GRETIL mbh_03_u.htm).
kept.evidence: sacred-texts.com returned 403 to my fetcher, so I checked the same Ganguli translation in Gutenberg #15474. The text says Indradyumna 'fell from heaven, crying, My achievements are lost!' and asks Markandeya 'Dost thou know me?'. Markandeya points to 'an owl of the name of Pravarakarna. He is older than I.' The owl points to 'a crane of the name of Nadijangha. He is older than we.' The crane points to 'a tortoise of the name of Akupara. He is older than I.' Then: 'his eyes were filled with tears ... This lake was excavated by the feet of the cows given away by this king unto the Brahmanas.' The moral verse: 'As long as that report lasts, so long is the doer said to be in heaven.' He also 'became a horse' to carry Markandeya. The GRETIL Sanskrit confirms 'nadijangho nama bakah' and 'akuparo nama kacchapah'. FIX: the draft's 'oldest of all' is implied by the chain, not stated, so I dropped it.
kept.safety: Royalty: in the text he is 'a royal sage' and 'king Indradyumna', and the lake carries his name. The retelling leaves all of this out. Leave out the tortoise's line about the sacrificial stake. The Sanskrit says the tortoise had been placed in his fire altars a thousand times, which is ritual harm. Also leave out the fall from heaven, the line about evil-doers in the lower regions, and the closing Nriga 'sunk in hell' line. Just say the man gave cows away, without 'to the Brahmanas'. Make no claim about long life coming from practice.
kept.joke_angle: In this story everyone says 'ask someone older'. In my shala, the someone older is now me. But I am not the tortoise who remembers everything. At 5 a.m. I cannot remember where I put my glasses.

kept.title: The serpent who holds the earth steady
kept.story: The story goes that the serpent Shesha, also called Ananta, 'the endless', went away to practise until he was only skin and bone. Brahma told him his hard practice was troubling all creatures, and offered a gift. Shesha asked only to keep loving goodness and practice, so Brahma, pleased, gave him a job: hold the earth steady on his head.
kept.asana: Not a series asana; this is a chant and sutra link. Tradition (a legend) holds that Patanjali is Ananta/Adishesha, honoured in the Ashtanga opening chant as 'sahasra-sirasam svetam' (thousand white, radiant heads). Yoga Sutra 2.47 names Ananta as a focus for steady asana, so it pairs with 2.46 'sthira sukham asanam' and with every asana.
kept.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Astika Parva), Section 36, trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896), Project Gutenberg #15474. Yoga Sutra 2.47, trans. James Haughton Woods, The Yoga-System of Patanjali, Harvard Oriental Series 17 (1914), p. 192, with Vachaspati Misra's gloss (https://archive.org/details/yogasystemofpata00wooduoft). Chant: ashtangayoga.info, 'Ashtanga Yoga Mantra' page (Dr. Ronald Steiner).
kept.evidence: Gutenberg #15474, Section XXXVI: Sesha, 'leaving his mother practised hard penances, living upon air'; 'his flesh, skin, and sinews dried up'; Brahma: 'thou art afflicting all creatures by thy hard penances'; Sesha's boon: 'may my heart always delight in virtue and in blessed ascetic penances'; Brahma: 'I am exceedingly gratified with this thy self-denial and love of peace ... Bear thou ... this Earth ... so that she may be steady'; Sesha: 'place her on my head'; and 'The snake, Sesha, the lord Ananta'. Woods p. 192, from the archive.org OCR: '47. By relaxation of effort or by a [mental] state-of-balance with reference to Ananta', glossed as 'Ananta, the Chief of Serpents, who upholds the globe of the earth upon his thousand very steadfast hoods'. Woods' footnote 'Ananta is Vasuki' conflicts with the Mahabharata, where Sesha is 'the elder brother of the king of the snakes', so do not repeat it. The ashtangayoga.info mantra page shows 'sahasra-sirasam svetam; pranamami patanjalim', glossed 'who has a thousand radiant heads'. FIX: in the text Brahma is pleased, not scolding. The draft's 'practised too hard' and 'original over-practiser' framing misreads the text and could look like mocking Adishesha, who is Patanjali in the lineage chant. I changed the title and the tone.
kept.safety: Leave out why he left home: the mother's curse that the serpents will burn in a sacrifice, his 'wicked' brothers, and his wish to 'cast off this body'. Do not present skin-and-bone austerity or 'living upon air' as advice: it is an old story, not a practice tip. Never frame Shesha/Patanjali as wrong or excessive. Label 'Patanjali is Adishesha' as tradition. It makes no health claim.
kept.joke_angle: Shesha practised so hard that all creatures felt it. When I practise hard at 5 a.m., only my neighbours feel it, through the wall, from my Ujjayi breathing.

kept.title: Patanjali fell into an old teacher's hands
kept.story: A legend: the yogini Gonika felt her life was near its end, with no one to receive her knowledge. She prayed to the Sun, water cupped in her palms. Opening her eyes, she saw a tiny snake there. It took human form and asked to be her son. She named him Patanjali: pata, fallen, anjali, joined palms.
kept.asana: Not a series asana. It links to the Ashtanga opening chant, said at the start of practice: 'praṇamāmi patañjalim' ('I bow to Patanjali'). The same verse describes him as human form to the shoulders with a thousand bright heads, which is the serpent of this legend.
kept.source: B.K.S. Iyengar, 'Legend of Sage Patanjali', official B.K.S. Iyengar website (bksiyengar.com). Opening chant: ashtangayoga.info Mantra practice sheet (English), (c) Dr. Ronald Steiner, 2015.
kept.evidence: Opened bksiyengar.com/modules/iyoga/legend.htm (header 'B K S Iyengar - Legend of Sage Patanjali'). Verbatim: Gonika is 'a yogini and tapasvini'; 'Gonika, thinking that her earthly life was approaching its end, had searched for a worthy son...But she had found no one'; 'She took a handful of water, as a final oblation to Him, closed her eyes and meditated on the Sun'; 'she saw a tiny snake moving in her palms who soon took on a human form'; 'This tiny male human prostrated to yogini Gonika and asked her to accept him as her son'; 'Pata means fallen or falling and Anjali means palms folded in prayer'. Every detail in the story matches. Prologue confirmed: Vishnu absorbed in Shiva's dance, Adisesa 'on the point of collapsing, gasping for breath'. The page does NOT mention Chidambaram or Vyaghrapada, so that note needs its own source if used. Extracted the ashtangayoga.info Mantra-EN PDF: 'ābāhu puruṣākāraṁ śankha-cakr-āsi dhāriṇam | sahasra śirasaṁ śvetaṁ praṇamāmi patañjalim', footer '(c) ashtangayoga.info Dr. Ronald Steiner, 2015'. Natarajasana is confirmed as no. 34 of the 3rd series on ashtangayoga.info. I found no classical primary text for the Gonika story itself, so it stays labelled a legend from Iyengar's retelling.
kept.safety: Passes. 'Near the end of her life' is about ageing, with no death scene and no victim. Do not translate the chant line about the conch, discus and sword (asi) on screen, because it brings in a weapon. Do not use the prologue joke about Vishnu getting heavy: it makes a god the butt of the joke even if Boonchu is the comparison. No health claims.
kept.joke_angle: Gonika joined her palms once and a student fell into them. Boonchu has joined his palms for the opening chant every morning for 20 years, and the only thing that has fallen into them is his reading glasses.

kept.title: Marichi, the ray of light that became a star
kept.story: Marichi means 'ray of light'. He is one of the seven sages. In Indian star-lore, the seven sages are the seven stars of the Big Dipper, and Marichi is the tip of the handle. A very old Vedic text says the seven sages were once called 'the Bears'. Iyengar wrote that Marichi was grandfather of the Sun god.
kept.asana: Marichyasana A, B, C and D, Primary series (Yoga Chikitsa). Confirmed on the ashtangayoga.info 1st series page.
kept.source: Monier-Williams, Sanskrit-English Dictionary (1899), p. 790, 'marīci': 'a particle of light, shining mote or speck in the air'; 'ray of light (of the sun or moon)'; Prajapati and one of the seven sages in one account; 'the star η in the great Bear' (citing Varahamihira's Brhat Samhita). Shatapatha Brahmana 2.1.2.4, trans. Julius Eggeling, Sacred Books of the East 12 (1882), pp. 282-283. B.K.S. Iyengar, Light on Yoga, Marichyasana I: 'Marichi was the grandfather of Surya (the Sun God).' (Drop the 'entry 64' number; see evidence.)
kept.evidence: Cologne MW scan: p. 790 gives 'ray of light', sage/Prajapati (one of the seven sages and father of Kashyapa in one account), and 'the star η in the great Bear, VarBrS'. Wikipedia 'Saptarishi' table: 'Marichi / η UMa / Alkaid', the end star of the handle. Eggeling SB 2.1.2.4 (sacred-texts mirror, sbe1241): 'for the seven Rishis were in former times [p. 283] called the Rikshas (bears)'. The page split 282/283 is confirmed. Light on Yoga: the quote is confirmed word for word in The Illustrated Light on Yoga (archive.org text): 'This asana is dedicated to the sage Marichi, son of the Creator, Brahma. Marichi was the grandfather of Surya (the Sun God).' That edition numbers it 34, and I could not open the 1966 edition (archive.org restricted), so the 'entry 64' number is unconfirmed and should be removed. This is the only fix: the story's facts all check out. ashtangayoga.info 1st series page lists Maricyasana A, B, C and D.
kept.safety: Passes if you keep only the 'Bears' sentence. The rest of SB 2.1.2.4 is about the sages' wives (the Pleiades) being kept from marital intercourse, so leave it out. No kings, no conflict, no health claims.
kept.joke_angle: The seven sages were once called 'the Bears'. At 5 a.m., before his coffee and his first Marichyasana D, the students say Boonchu still is one.

kept.title: A hundred autumns: the long-life prayer in Vasistha's book
kept.story: The seventh book of the Rig Veda is credited to the sage Vasistha. One hymn there has a simple wish about the rising Sun: 'A hundred autumns may we see that bright eye, god-ordained, arise: A hundred autumns may we live.' An autumn here means a year. Ashtanga practice still opens by saluting the Sun, in Surya Namaskara.
kept.asana: Vasisthasana, first asana of the 3rd series (Advanced A, Sthira Bhaga). It also links to Surya Namaskara, which opens every series. Note: ashtangayoga.info warns that older Ashtanga books often swap the names Vasisthasana and Visvamitrasana, so check which image you use.
kept.source: Rig Veda 7.66.16, trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith, The Hymns of the Rigveda, Vol. III (Benares: E. J. Lazarus and Co., 1891), p. 86. Griffith's note to RV 7.1: 'All the hymns of this Book are ascribed to the Rishi Vasishtha, with whom his sons are associated as the seers of parts of two hymns.'
kept.evidence: sacred-texts.com returned 403 (Cloudflare), so I checked the archive.org scan text (hymnsrigveda01grifgoog, title page 'VOL. III. BENARES: E. J. LAZARUS AND CO. 1891'; archive metadata wrongly says 1920). Page 86 reads: '16 A hundred autumns may we see that bright eye, god-ordained, arise: A hundred autumns may we live.' Verse 15 just before it: 'The seven sister bays bear Surya on his car', so the 'eye' is the Sun. The Book 7 note is confirmed word for word. Vedapath also lists the rishi of 7.66.16 as Vasistha and the deity as Surya. One fix in the notes: page 86 has no Griffith footnote on verse 16, so the claim that 'Griffith notes' other Vedic texts with this wish is not confirmed and should be dropped. Vasisthasana is no. 1 of the 3rd series on ashtangayoga.info.
kept.safety: Passes. The same book has the battle hymns (Griffith's Hymn XXXIII mentions 'the fight with the ten kings') and 7.66 verse 6 mentions 'our princes', so quote only verse 16. Leave out the Vasistha and Vishvamitra quarrel. Present the line as an old prayer, not as a promise that practice adds years to your life.
kept.joke_angle: At 53, Boonchu is past the halfway mark of his hundred autumns. Good news: he has watched the sun rise from his mat thousands of times. Bad news: his hamstrings have not risen with it once.

kept.title: The old couple in the sky: Vasistha and Arundhati
kept.story: In the Big Dipper, the sage Vasistha's star has a faint partner, Arundhati, his wife. Astronomers call them Mizar and Alcor. An old Vedic wedding guide says that when the bride sees the polar star, Arundhati and the seven sages, she ends her silence and says: 'May my husband live and I get offspring (children).'
kept.asana: Vasisthasana, first asana of the 3rd series (Advanced A, Sthira Bhaga). The 'hundred autumns' story above uses the same asana, so post them as a pair or on different days.
kept.source: Asvalayana Grihya Sutra 1.7.22, trans. Hermann Oldenberg, The Grihya-Sutras Part I, Sacred Books of the East 29 (Oxford, 1886), p. 170. Monier-Williams, Sanskrit-English Dictionary (1899), p. 88, 'arundhatī'. Mizar/Alcor identification: Wikipedia 'Saptarishi', citing P. N. Shankar, A Guide to the Night Sky (1985).
kept.evidence: Oldenberg scan text (running head 'I ADHYAYA, 7 KANDIKA', p. 170): '22. When she sees the polar-star, the star Arundhati, and the seven Rishis (ursa major), let her break the silence (and say), "May my husband live and I get offspring."' Also 1.7.19 ends 'Let us acquire many sons who may reach old age!' (p. 169-170). Cologne MW p. 88: 'the little and scarcely visible star Alcor'; 'the wife of Vasishtha'; 'at marriage ceremonies Arundhati is invoked as a pattern of conjugal excellence by the bridegroom'; and 'a kind of super natural faculty (also called kundalini)'. Wikipedia Saptarishi: 'Vasishtha / ζ UMa / Mizar' and 'Vasishtha is accompanied by Arundhati, a faint companion star (Alcor/80 Ursa Majoris)', citing Shankar 1985 nearby (the table itself has no citation). All story details match.
kept.safety: Passes. Leave out the folk belief about not seeing Arundhati before death, and 1.7.21 (the old woman 'whose husband is alive and whose children are alive'). I replaced the suggested joke about Boonchu's wife: it guesses at his private life and pulls another person into the joke. No health claims.
kept.joke_angle: Vasistha's star has stood perfectly still in the sky for 3,000 years. Boonchu holds Vasisthasana for five breaths and wobbles on every one of them.

kept.title: The frogs who wake with the rain
kept.story: A Rig Veda hymn (7.103) sings about frogs. "They who lay quiet for a year, the Brahmans who fulfil their vows," wake up when the rain comes. One frog repeats another's call, "as he who learns the lesson of the teacher." At the end, the poet thanks the frogs for the rainy season, with its "cows in hundreds" and longer lives.
kept.asana: Bhekasana (frog), Intermediate series (Nadi Shodhana), between Shalabhasana and Dhanurasana. Confirmed on the AshtangaYoga.info Intermediate vinyasa sheet and on David Robson's Intermediate series chart (NCSU). The only link is the frog image: the hymn says nothing about any asana.
kept.source: Rig Veda 7.103, stanzas 1, 5 and 10, trans. Ralph T. H. Griffith, The Hymns of the Rigveda, Vol. III (Benares: E. J. Lazarus and Co., 1891), pp. 125-126. The scan is at archive.org/details/hymnsrigveda01grifgoog. Its catalogue record says 1920, but the title page in the scan says Vol. III, 1891.
kept.evidence: sacred-texts.com returned 403 to both WebFetch and curl, so I checked the 1891 scan instead. Title page: 'THE HYMNS OF THE RIGVEDA ... VOL. III. BENARES: E. J. LAZARUS AND CO. 1891', with Book VII on pp. 1-230. Hymn CIII 'Frogs' starts on p. 125 and runs onto p. 126, and the index lists 'Frogs, 125,126'. Stanza 1: 'They who lay quiet for a year, the Brahmans who fulfil their vows, The frogs have lifted up their voice, the voice Parjanya hath inspired.' Stanza 3: 'at the coming of the Rains'. Stanza 5: 'When one of these repeats the other's language, as he who learns the lesson of the teacher.' Stanza 10: 'The frogs who give us cows in hundreds lengthen our lives in this most fertilizing season.' Griffith's note on stanza 10 explains that the frogs are 'the earliest proclaimers of the advent of the Rains which revive and fertilise the earth.' Griffith's note on the hymn quotes Max Muller: 'clearly a satire on the priests'. The quotes in the draft are accurate, and the draft's 'lying silent' is a fair paraphrase of 'lay quiet'.
kept.safety: Tell it only as a rain hymn. Don't use the Max Muller reading (a satire on priests), and don't make any joke that compares priests to frogs. Present the 'lengthen our lives' line only as the poet's thanks for the rainy season. Never say that Bhekasana, or Ashtanga, lengthens your life: the draft's fit line 'it lengthens your life' is an overstated health claim and must go. There is no violence, royalty or conflict in the hymn.
kept.joke_angle: The frogs stay silent for a whole year, then sing when the rain comes. Boonchu's knees stay silent all year, then sing every morning in Bhekasana, rainy season or not.

kept.title: Matsyendra, the fish who stayed still and listened
kept.story: A legend, as B.K.S. Iyengar tells it: Shiva explained the secrets of yoga to Parvati on a lonely island. A fish near the shore heard everything. It listened with full attention and did not move. Shiva saw that the fish had learned yoga, sprinkled water on it, and it became Matsyendra, "Lord of the Fishes", who then spread yoga.
kept.asana: Ardha Matsyendrasana, Intermediate series, after Bharadvajasana and before Eka Pada Sirsasana (confirmed on the AshtangaYoga.info sheet and the Robson chart). Purna Matsyendrasana, Advanced A (third series, Sthira Bhaga), after Astavakrasana (confirmed in the AshtangaYoga.info third-series list).
kept.source: Legend: B.K.S. Iyengar, Light on Yoga (London: George Allen & Unwin, 1966), under Ardha Matsyendrasana I. I checked the wording in The Illustrated Light on Yoga, the abridged edition of the same text, entry 55, p. 112. I could not confirm the entry number '116' in the draft, so leave it out. For comparison, the yoga-text claim is the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, ch. 1, Matsyendrasana verses, trans. Pancham Sinh (Allahabad, first published 1915, not 1914). Sinh numbers these verses 28-29; modern editions number them 1.26-27. For background: Wikipedia 'Matsyendranatha', fl. early 10th century.
kept.evidence: In The Illustrated Light on Yoga (archive.org copy), p. 112, entry 55 Ardha Matsyendrasana: 'It is related that once Lord Siva went to a lonely island and explained to his consort Parvati the mysteries of Yoga. A fish near the shore heard everything with concentration and remained motionless while listening. Siva, realizing that the fish had learnt Yoga, sprinkled water upon it, and immediately the fish gained divine form and became Matsyendra (Lord of the Fishes) and thereafter spread the knowledge of Yoga.' The copyright page says the book was first published by George Allen & Unwin in 1966. The draft story matches this. Pancham Sinh (DLI copy, preface dated Ajmer, 31 January 1915; the Munshiram reprint says 'First published 1915'), verses 28-29: 'It increases appetite and is an instrument for destroying the group of the most deadly diseases. Its practice awakens the Kundalini, stops the nectar shedding from the moon in people.' Note that the verse says 'stops the nectar shedding', not 'steadies the moon', and that it describes the full Matsyendrasana, not Ardha. Wikipedia 'Matsyendranath' redirects to 'Matsyendranatha', which gives 'fl. early 10th century'. It also cites the Feuerstein 'sleepy spouse' quote and the version where the parents throw the baby into the ocean.
kept.safety: Label it a legend and Iyengar's retelling: it is not in the Hatha Yoga Pradipika. Leave out the variant where the parents throw the baby into the ocean (harm to a child). Leave out Feuerstein's 'sleepy spouse' line, because it can read as mocking Parvati. Never present the Hatha Yoga Pradipika lines ('destroying ... the most deadly diseases', awakening Kundalini) as fact; if they go to the misconceptions team, they are an example of an old text overpromising. Change the draft's fit line 'taught for decades' to the true figure, 20 years of practice. The joke targets Boonchu's talking, never the fish, Shiva or Parvati.
kept.joke_angle: A fish learned all of yoga by staying still and silent. Boonchu has 20 years of practice and still can't stay silent for five breaths in Ardha Matsyendrasana. He does stay silent at 5 a.m., but only because he isn't awake yet.

kept.title: The old monkey whose tail would not move
kept.story: In the Mahabharata, the strong hero Bhima finds an old monkey lying across a mountain path. The monkey says he is too old to get up, so Bhima can just move his tail aside. Bhima pulls with one hand, then both, sweating. The tail does not move. The monkey is Hanuman, his elder brother. Both are sons of the wind god.
kept.asana: Hanumanasana, Advanced A (third series), after Ganda Bherundasana and before Supta Trivikramasana (confirmed in the AshtangaYoga.info third-series list). The asana is named after Hanuman, not after this tail episode, so the link is the character.
kept.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Sections 146-148, trans. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896), Project Gutenberg eBook #15474 (Volume 1, Books 1-3). Section 146 has the tail. Section 147 has the boon: 'may I live as long as the history of thy deeds remaineth extant on earth!' and Rama's answer 'So be it'. In Section 148, Bhima says 'now have I seen my elder brother'.
kept.evidence: sacred-texts.com returned 403 for m03146 and m03147, so I downloaded Gutenberg #15474 and read Section CXLVI. The quote is exact: 'In consequence of age, I have no strength to get up. From pity for me, do thou go, moving aside my tail.' Bhima 'took hold of the tail with his left hand; but could not move that tail ... Then with both arms he pulled it ... his body was covered with sweat; and yet he could not raise it.' He then bows with joined hands and says 'I ask thee as a disciple'. Both are called offspring of the wind-god. Section CXLVII has the boon exactly as the draft quotes it. Section CXLVIII: 'bowed unto his brother, Hanuman ... now have I seen my elder brother.' The same section also says Hanuman lay in a plantain (banana) wood on the path. The draft is accurate. The only change is that 'the strongest man in the Mahabharata' becomes 'the strong hero'.
kept.safety: In the source, Bhima announces himself as a Kshatriya of the Kuru race, threatens the monkey ('I shall send thee to the abode of Yama') and plans to send him 'to the region of Yama' by the tail. Leave out the prince identity and all the threats. Section 147 retells the abduction of Sita, the burning of Lanka and the killing of Ravana, so if the boon is used, give only Hanuman's wish and Rama's 'So be it'. Hanuman is a deity: Boonchu should not play or claim to be Hanuman. The joke must be about Boonchu's real age, never about Hanuman's. No health claim.
kept.joke_angle: Hanuman only pretended he was too old to get up. At 53, at 5 a.m., Boonchu is not pretending.

kept.title: Jambavan: 'we are on the other shore of our age'
kept.story: In the Ramayana, the monkey army must jump across the sea: a hundred yojanas, an old unit of distance. The leaders can leap ten, twenty, up to eighty. Jambavan the bear, the oldest, says his strength in youth had no equal, but now he can do only ninety. Then he turns to quiet Hanuman: "Arise... leap over this vast ocean."
kept.asana: Hanumanasana, Advanced A (third series), confirmed in the AshtangaYoga.info third-series list. It recalls the leap across the sea that follows this scene. Supta Trivikramasana and Utthita Trivikramasana are also in Advanced A (confirmed), but their link runs through verse 4-65-15, which names Emperor Bali, so leave it out.
kept.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda, Sarga 65, verses 3-17, and Sarga 66, verses 1-2 and 34-36, trans. Desiraju Hanumanta Rao, valmikiramayan.net. The Sarga 65 page says '© Mar, 2003 ... Revised: Jan 05' and the Sarga 66 page says '© April, 2003'. The draft's 'completed 2006' does not appear on these pages, so cite 2003, revised 2005.
kept.evidence: Opened and read the Sarga 65 and 66 pages. The leaders' distances are 4-65-3 Gaja 10 and Gavaaksha 20, then Sharabha 30, Rishabha 40, Gandhamaadana 50, Mainda 60, Dvivida 70 and Sushena 80. 4-65-10 calls Jambavan 'the oldest one among all of them'. 4-65-11: 'we are presently on the other shore of our age'. 4-65-13: 'we can go up to ninety yojana-s, undoubtedly'. 4-65-16: 'I am presently old and decrepit ... though my energy in youth was unmatchable and unsurpassable.' 4-65-17: 'by that much endeavour that task will be unaccomplished'. In 4-65-19, Angada names the hundred yojanas. 4-66-2: 'Hanuma, why do not you mumble something, why do you resort to a calmly loneliness'. 4-66-34: 'I am now aged and my valiance is completely lessened ... you alone are endowed with all endowments among us'. 4-66-36: 'Arise, oh, lion-like monkey, leap over this vast ocean'. All the draft's numbers and quotes match.
kept.safety: Leave out Angada (a prince), Sugriva ('king of monkeys') and the reason for the crossing (Sita taken by Ravana). Also leave out the translator's note that the monkeys were held back by fear of Ravana, and Emperor Bali (4-65-15). Sarga 66 also tells Hanuman's birth story, which includes a curse on Anjana and the young Hanuman being struck down; leave that out too. Don't claim that Hanumanasana keeps you young or is safe at any age. The joke stays on Boonchu and never on Jambavan's age.
kept.joke_angle: Jambavan was honest: age took ten yojanas from his jump. Age took about ten centimetres from Boonchu's Hanumanasana, and with his hamstrings he is still waiting, every morning at 6 a.m., for them to come back.

kept.title: Bharadvaja asks for a fourth lifetime of study
kept.story: A legend from a Vedic text. Bharadvaja studied the Vedas for three lifetimes. When he was old and weak, the god Indra offered him a fourth life. He said he would spend it studying. Indra showed him three mountain-like shapes, took one handful from each and said: 'The Vedas are infinite. This is what you studied in three lives.'
kept.asana: Bharadvajasana, Ashtanga Intermediate series (Nadi Shodhana), placed after Bakasana and before Ardha Matsyendrasana. The asana is dedicated to the sage Bharadvaja, but the twist itself is a modern (20th century) shape, so do not say the sage practised it.
kept.source: Taittiriya Brahmana 3.10.11.3-5. Sanskrit and English in John Muir, Original Sanskrit Texts, vol. 3 (The Vedas), 2nd ed., revised and enlarged (London: Trubner & Co., 1868), pp. 16-17. Series check: ashtangayoga.info Intermediate Series cheat sheet (R. Steiner, 2015).
kept.evidence: Opened the archive.org full text of Muir vol. 3 (title page: 'Volume Third ... Second Edition, Revised and Enlarged ... London: Trubner & Co.'; Illinois copy catalogued 1868). Pp. 16-17 give the Sanskrit of TB iii.10.11.3-5 and the translation word for word as quoted: 'Bharadvaja lived through three lives in the state of a religious student. Indra approached him when he was lying old and decrepit ... if I give thee a fourth life, how wilt thou employ it? I will lead the life of a religious student ... He showed him three mountain-like objects, as it were unknown. From each of them he took a handful ... These are the Vedas. The Vedas are infinite. This is what thou hast studied during these three lives.' Sanskrit has 'anantah vai vedah'. Verse 5: Indra teaches him Agni Savitra and he 'became immortal'. Note Muir's footnote 18: 'three lives' may mean one life three times the normal length, not three births. Downloaded ashtangayoga.info IntermediateSeries-EN.pdf: Bharadvajasana is listed in 2nd series. Wikipedia and iHanuman confirm the asana is dedicated to the sage Bharadvaja and is a 20th century form.
kept.safety: Clean: no war, violence, royalty or conflict. Indra is shown respectfully as the teacher. Leave out the 'became immortal' line, or label it clearly as myth, so it never reads as a promise that practice extends life. No health claims. If you mention Iyengar's note that Bharadvaja was the father of Drona, skip it: it leads straight into the Mahabharata war.
kept.joke_angle: Bharadvaja put in three lifetimes and got one handful. Boonchu has put in twenty years of 5 a.m. alarms, and the handful he is holding is still his own stiff hamstrings.

kept.title: Hanuman's wish: live as long as the story is told
kept.story: A legend from the last book of the Ramayana. Hanuman asked Rama for one wish: to stay alive for as long as people on earth tell Rama's story. Rama hugged him and said it would be so. That is why tradition calls Hanuman a chiranjeevi, a long-lived one, still here while the story is told.
kept.asana: Hanumanasana (front splits), Ashtanga Advanced A (third series, Sthira Bhaga), placed after Supta Trivikramasana. The asana is named after Hanuman, not after this wish, so say 'named after Hanuman' rather than 'named for this story'.
kept.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Uttara Kanda, sarga 40 in the southern/vulgate numbering (Hari Prasad Shastri tr., ch. 40, 'Rama takes leave of the Bears, Monkeys and Titans'); verses 7.39.15-19 in the critical edition. English: Manmatha Nath Dutt, The Ramayana vol. 4: Uttara Kanda (Calcutta, 1894), Section L (printed 'XLX'), with the promise repeated in Section CXXI. Series check: ashtangayoga.info Advanced A cheat sheet.
kept.evidence: Opened Gutenberg #62496 (title page: Calcutta, 1894). The contents list runs XLIX, XLX, LI, which confirms the misprint for L. The quote is word for word: 'May my life remain in my body as long as the stories of Rama shall be in currency on earth.' Then Rama 'rose up from his throne and having embraced Hanuman affectionately said ... As long as my stories shall be current on earth thy fame shall exist and life shall be in thy body.' Section CXXI: 'It is settled that thou shalt live forever ... As long as my history shall run current in this world'. The Sanskrit (sanskritdocuments.org, Tokunaga/critical text) has it at sarga 39.16-19: 'yaavad raamakathaam viira shrosye 'ham prthiviitale / taavac chariire vatsyantu mama praanaah'. Wisdomlib's Shastri translation (southern recension) has the same scene in chapter 40. Advanced A PDF lists Hanumanasana.
kept.safety: Safe as retold. In the source, Hanuman calls Rama 'O king' and Rama rises from his throne. Keep Rama as the hero with no throne or court, and do not mention the war. 'Chiranjeevi' is labelled as tradition, which is correct: the list of chiranjeevis comes from later tradition, not this verse. Hanuman is a deity, so the joke stays on Boonchu's splits and never on Hanuman. Do not use the leap to Lanka as the origin story, because it sits inside the war. No health claims.
kept.joke_angle: Hanuman lives as long as the story is told. Boonchu's front splits also live in a story, the one he has told every year for twenty years. It is called 'next year'.

kept.title: The fish who heard the first yoga lesson
kept.story: A legend of the yogis. Shiva taught yoga to Parvati by the sea, and Parvati fell asleep. But a listener in the form of a fish heard every word, so he was called Matsyendra, 'Lord of the Fishes'. The Hatha Yoga Pradipika names Matsyendra among the first masters of hatha yoga, and two twists in Ashtanga carry his name.
kept.asana: Ardha Matsyendrasana, Ashtanga Intermediate series (after Bharadvajasana). Purna Matsyendrasana, Advanced A (third series, after Ashtavakrasana). Both confirmed on the ashtangayoga.info series sheets.
kept.source: George Weston Briggs, Gorakhnath and the Kanphata Yogis (Calcutta: YMCA Publishing House; London: Oxford University Press, 1938), p. 152 (Parvati asleep, Matsyendranath in fish form), p. 182 (Nepal: seashore, Matsyendra as fish listening) and pp. 231-232 (Nepal version with Lokeshvara). Hatha Yoga Pradipika 1.4-5 and 1.28-29, tr. Pancham Sinh, Sacred Books of the Hindus vol. XV pt. III (Allahabad: Panini Office, 1915; often cited as 1914). Most other editions number these 1.26-27.
kept.evidence: Opened the Briggs full text on archive.org (metadata: 1938). P. 152: 'it was because a certain Matsyendranath, in the form of a fish, overheard Siva as he expounded the teaching ... (Parvati went to sleep while Siva was expounding the doctrine.)' P. 182 (Nepal): Siva 'recited the Yoga doctrine to Parvati, standing on the sea shore, while Matsyendra (in the form of a fish) was listening'. Pp. 231-232 (Nepal): 'She fell asleep while Siva was speaking, but Lokesvar heard it, disguised in the form of a fish. He is consequently known as Matsyendranatha.' So 'the fish became Matsyendra' was inaccurate: the listener was already Matsyendra (or Lokeshvara) in fish form, and the name came from that. The draft also left out p. 152, which is the citation without the Buddhist identification. Pancham Sinh scan: verse 4 'Matsyendra, Goraksa, etc., knew Hatha Vidya'; verse 5 lists siddhas starting 'Sri Adinatha (Siva), Matsyendra'; verses 28-29 give the asana 'as explained by Sri Matsyanatha. It increases appetite and is an instrument for destroying the group of the most deadly diseases. Its practice awakens the Kundalini'. That scan's preface is signed Ajmer, 31 January 1915. Indicayoga's overview confirms 1.26-27 in standard numbering.
kept.safety: Tell Parvati falling asleep plainly and gently, as a detail of the legend, and never as the punchline. If unsure, cut that clause; the story still works. Drop the old 'fish who stayed awake' framing, because it sets the goddess up as the comic contrast. Avoid the Nepal detail that Avalokiteshvara taught Shiva yoga: Briggs ties it to 'the struggle between Buddhism and Saivism in Nepal', which is religious conflict. Leave out the other Matsyendra legends (a king's unburnt navel swallowed by a fish, the Ceylon queen, entering a dead king's body), which bring in death and royalty. Do not repeat the HYP claim that the twist destroys 'the most deadly diseases' or awakens Kundalini as fact, and do not use it as an overpromise beat either. At most say 'old texts made big promises; modern studies have not tested them'.
kept.joke_angle: A fish heard one lesson and got two twists named after him. Boonchu has heard 'soften your hamstrings' every morning for twenty years, and his hamstrings still haven't heard it.

kept.title: The sage called Hairy who would not build a house
kept.story: An Indian story tells of a hermit named Lomasha, or 'Hairy'. His chest hair grew in a ring, bare in the middle: one hair falls each time the era of one Indra, a sky god, ends. Feeling 'short-lived', he chose 'to possess no home, to build no house', and carried only an umbrella of grass.
kept.asana: None. The story has no asana link, so don't invent one.
kept.source: Brahmavaivarta Purana, Krishna-janma Khanda 47.50-161, as retold by Heinrich Zimmer, Myths and Symbols in Indian Art and Civilization, ed. Joseph Campbell (New York: Pantheon, Bollingen Series VI, 1946), ch. 1 'The Parade of Ants', pp. 3-11; the hermit is on pp. 8-9. The Sanskrit name Lomasha ('the hairy one') comes from S. Jayanarayanan's English translation of the same chapter, posted to the Advaita-l list on 15 Jul 2003 (a secondary source).
kept.evidence: I read the full text of the archive.org scan. Its metadata confirms Zimmer, ed. Campbell, Pantheon, 1946, from the Delhi University Library copy. 'The Parade of Ants' starts on p. 3. On p. 8 the hermit has 'a paltry parasol of grass' and 'a quaint, circular cluster of hair' that is 'intact at the circumference' but missing at the center. On pp. 8-9 he says: 'Hairy is my name ... Since I know that I am short-lived, I have decided to possess no home, to build no house, and neither to marry nor to seek a livelihood ... With the fall of an Indra, one hair drops.' On p. 10: 'It had been the god Shiva himself.' The p. 11 footnote reads 'Brahmavaivarta Purana, Krishna-janma Khanda, 47.50-161'. Zimmer only says 'Hairy'. The Advaita-l translation has 'My name is Lomasha (the hairy one)' and also says he was Shiva. Every claim in the draft matches.
kept.safety: Safe if told as written. Leave out Zimmer's opening (Indra slays the dragon), Indra's palace, Vishvakarman, the queen, and every 'king of the gods' phrase. Leave out the hermit's line about when he himself will die, and the Shiva reveal (or mention it only respectfully). This is not the Mahabharata's pilgrim-guide Lomasha. No health claims. IMPORTANT: Sharath Jois died in November 2024 at 53, Boonchu's age now. Don't build any joke on Boonchu being 'short-lived' or running out of years at 53. That includes the draft's 'plenty of time at 53' angle; aim the joke at his hamstrings instead.
kept.joke_angle: Lomasha loses one chest hair each time a whole era of the gods ends. My hamstrings open at about the same speed: twenty years of early mornings, and the first era still hasn't ended.

kept.title: Markandeya: thousands of years old, looks 25
kept.story: In a story from the Mahabharata, India's great old epic, the sage Markandeya arrives 'grown grey in the practise of penances' (long spiritual discipline). He 'had seen many thousand years of life', yet 'signs of old age he had none'. In fact, 'he looked like one only twenty-five years old'.
kept.asana: None. The text says penances (tapas), not asana practice, so don't link it to any asana.
kept.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Markandeya-Samasya Parva, Section CLXXXII, tr. Kisari Mohan Ganguli (1883-1896). The same text is also on Project Gutenberg, eBook #15474 (The Mahabharata, vol. 1).
kept.evidence: sacred-texts.com returned 403 to automated fetches, so I checked the same Ganguli translation in Project Gutenberg #15474. The heading '(Markandeya-Samasya Parva)' sits under Section CLXXXI, and the passage is in Section CLXXXII. Exact words: 'there appeared then the saint Markandeya, grown grey in the practise of penances. And he had seen many thousand years of life ... Signs of old age he had none; and deathless he was ... And he looked like one only twenty-five years old.' All four quoted phrases match, and so do the section number and the translator.
kept.safety: Safe if told as written. In this scene Krishna and the Pandavas are present, and the lines just before it talk about armies and Duryodhana. Leave all of that out. Don't use 'deathless he was'. Skip the 'forever sixteen' Markandeya legend, where Shiva strikes Yama. Don't quote the chiranjeevi prayer verse as scripture, or as a promise of a hundred years free of illness: its source is unverified and it names rulers and warriors. No health claims. Never suggest that practice makes you look 25. Also given Sharath died at 53, avoid any 'deathless/immortal' joke tied to Boonchu's age.
kept.joke_angle: The Mahabharata says Markandeya went grey from practice and still looked twenty-five. After twenty years of dark-morning alarm clocks, I have finished the first half of that bio.

kept.title: Bhusunda, the old crow who watched his breath
kept.story: An Indian text, the Yoga Vasishtha, tells the story of Bhusunda, an old crow in a wish-granting tree on Mount Meru. He was 'beauteous even in old age', and no one had lived longer. His secret, he said, was watching his breath. Following every inhale and exhale, he found his life 'as interminable' (endless) as his breathing.
kept.asana: None. The only link is the breath: Ashtanga ties every movement to the breath (vinyasa), but the story names no asana. Don't call Bakasana 'crow', because baka means crane and a crow is kaka. Navasana in the joke is a real Primary Series asana.
kept.source: Yoga Vasishtha, Book VI (Nirvana Prakarana). The quotes are from ch. XIV v. 9-10 and ch. XXIV v. 13 and v. 35, tr. Vihari-Lala Mitra, The Yoga-Vasishtha Maharamayana of Valmiki, vol. 3 part 2 (Calcutta, 1891-1899); Project Gutenberg eBook #46531.
kept.evidence: Opened Gutenberg #46531 (Vol. 3 Part 2, translator Viharilala Mitra), headed 'NIRVANA-PRAKARANA. BOOK VI'. Ch. XIV: v. 6 has a kalpa (wish-granting) mango tree on the north-east summit of Meru, and v. 8 'one old raven by name of Bhusunda'. v. 9: 'There is no one in the womb of this world so long lived as he'. v. 10: 'This crony crow was beauteous even in old age'. Ch. XXIV v. 13: 'cogitation of vital breath, which has the cause of Bhusunda's longevity'. v. 35: 'by watching the motion of those airs (i.e. of the prana and apana--inspiration and expiration for the whole of my lifetime); I find the course of my life to be as interminable, as that of the continuity of my breathings.' All quotes and verse numbers match.
kept.safety: Safe if told as written. Skip the chapters where he survives the ends of world-ages (cosmic flood and fire), his birth story with the goddesses, and the framing with the prince Rama. Ch. XXIV v. 38 claims that pranayama lengthens life. That is the text's own claim, not evidence, so present the longevity only as part of the story and never say breathwork makes you live longer.
kept.joke_angle: Bhusunda watched his breath for ages and found it endless. The only place my breath feels endless is Navasana, where five breaths somehow get longer every year.

kept.title: Pick your age: the pool and the jam
kept.story: In an old Vedic story, the sage Chyavana was left on earth 'decrepit and ghostlike' (very old and weak). The healer twins, the Ashvins, told his wife to take him into a pool, 'and he shall come forth with whatever age he shall desire'. He did. A later Ayurveda text, the Charaka Samhita, also credits a herbal jam: Chyavanaprash.
kept.asana: None. Neither text links to any asana.
kept.source: Shatapatha Brahmana 4.1.5.1 and 4.1.5.12, tr. Julius Eggeling, Sacred Books of the East vol. 26 (Oxford, 1885), pp. 272-275. Charaka Samhita, Chikitsa Sthana 1.1.62-74, verse 72 ('asya prayogāc cyavanaḥ suvṛddho 'bhūt punar yuvā'), English by R. H. Singh et al. at https://www.carakasamhitaonline.com/index.php/Rasayana_Adhyaya. Note that Charaka Chikitsa 1.4.39-51 also credits the Ashvins with making Chyavana young again.
kept.evidence: Eggeling SBE 26, 4.1.5.1: Kyavana 'was left behind here (on earth) decrepit and ghostlike'. 4.1.5.8: the Asvins 'wandered about here on earth performing cures'. 4.1.5.12: 'They said, "Take him down to yonder pool, and he shall come forth with whatever age he shall desire!" She took him down to that pool, and he came forth with the age he desired.' Eggeling's footnote gives a possible other reading, 'Throw him into yonder pool', and says the Kanva version mentions only water. Charaka Ci 1.1.72, English: 'By consuming this Rasayana preparation, the extremely old sage Chyavana regained youthful age.' However, Charaka Ci 1.4.39-51 says Chyavana 'was reverted to youthful age' by the Ashvins. So the draft's 'instead' overstates the contrast, and I changed it to 'also'. Everything else matches.
kept.safety: Fixed one wording overstatement ('instead'). Leave out: the boys pelting the sage with clods (4.1.5.2), the fighting he caused, 'father fought with son' (4.1.5.3), the chieftain father, the chariot, the daughter given as atonement (4.1.5.6-7), the Ashvins trying to win her love (4.1.5.8-9), and the sacrifice dispute (4.1.5.13-15). Charaka 1.1.73-74 promises 'freedom from disease, longevity' and says the user 'gets rid of senility'. Those are claims made in the text, not clinical evidence. Never say the jam or a swim reverses ageing, and don't name or promote any commercial brand. This is the same sage as the anthill candidate, so use one or pair them.
kept.joke_angle: Chyavana stepped into a pool and came out at any age he wanted. I'm not greedy. I'd step in and ask for one thing: hamstrings that reach my toes before 7 a.m.

kept.title: Gorakhnath, the boy found in a dung heap
kept.story: A legend from Nepal: Shiva gave a woman something to eat and promised her a son. She threw it on a dung heap instead. Twelve years later the sage Matsyendra came by and asked to see the child. She searched the heap and found a boy of twelve. He became Gorakhnath, Matsyendra's loyal student.
kept.asana: Loose link, confirmed. HYP 1.55-56 (Sinh) describes Bhadrasana: heels on either side of the perineum, feet held firmly together with both hands. HYP 1.57: 'The expert Yogis call this Goraksa asana.' The nearest Ashtanga shape is Baddha Konasana, Primary series, right after Kukkutasana (ashtangayoga.info list). Some editions number these verses 1.53-54.
kept.source: G. W. Briggs, Gorakhnath and the Kanphata Yogis (Calcutta: Y.M.C.A. Publishing House; London: Humphrey Milford, Oxford University Press, 1938), pp. 182-183. Hatha Yoga Pradipika 1.55-57 and 1.63, tr. Pancham Sinh (Allahabad: Panini Office, Sacred Books of the Hindus vol. XV part III; usually cited as 1914, the scan I opened is dated January 1915).
kept.evidence: Opened the full Briggs text on archive.org. Title page confirms Y.M.C.A. Publishing House, Calcutta, and Humphrey Milford, Oxford University Press, 1938. p. 182: 'From Nepal comes the story that Siva ... gave something to a woman to eat, with a promise that she would obtain a son. The woman did not eat the substance, but cast it upon a dung-hill. Twelve years later, Matsyendra passed by the same spot and asked to see the child ... She there discovered a boy of twelve years. That boy was named Gorakhnath. Matsyendranath became his spiritual master and he served as a dutiful disciple.' The same page has the Panjab legend that he 'was born of dung'. pp. 182-183 has the Tahqiqat-i-Chishti variant: ashes from Siva's dhuni (sacred fire) thrown on a dung-hill. Opened Sinh's HYP scan on archive.org: 1.57 and 1.63 read exactly as quoted. 1.63 in full: 'As said by Goraksa, one should keep aloof from the society of the evil-minded, fire, women, travelling, early morning bath, fasting, and all kinds of bodily exertion.' All draft facts match.
kept.safety: Passes with care. No violence or harm. Tell the dung heap warmly, not as a gross-out, and keep Shiva, Matsyendra and the boy out of the joke. Do not repeat HYP 1.56's claim that Bhadrasana 'is the destroyer of all the diseases', which is an overstated health claim. If you use the HYP 1.63 'don't overdo it' line, quote only 'keep aloof from ... all kinds of bodily exertion', because the full list also names women. Leave out the other variant in Briggs p. 183 where Gorakhnath is a son of Shiva by a cow.
kept.joke_angle: Use skeleton 38, 'The exact number': 'Gorakhnath needed twelve years to show up. I have given my hamstrings twenty. They still haven't.' The laugh lands on Boonchu's stiff hamstrings, never on the boy, the heap or Matsyendra.

kept.title: Tirumular: one verse a year for 3,000 years
kept.story: The story goes that the Tamil yogi Tirumular sat in meditation under a pipal tree at Tiruvavaduthurai. Once a year he came out to write one verse. After 3,000 years he had the Tirumantiram, a classic of Tamil Shaiva yoga. Scholars date the book far later. It names seven chief asanas, including Padma (lotus) and Gomukha.
kept.asana: Added, because the draft had none. Tirumantiram, Tantra 3 (tr. B. Natarajan, Himalayan Academy web edition; verse numbers vary by edition): 559 Padmasana, 561 Kukkudasana (feet on the thighs, body raised), 563 'Bhadra, Gomukha, Padma and Simha, Svastika, Veera, and Sukha: these seven are asanas eminent and ancient'. Ashtanga matches checked on ashtangayoga.info: Kukkutasana in the Primary series, Gomukhasana A and B in the Intermediate series, Baddha Padmasana and Padmasana in the finishing sequence.
kept.source: Sekkizhar, Periya Puranam (12th century), Tirumula Nayanar Puranam (Tamil verse wording checked via tamil.wiki). Retelling: Sri Ramanasramam, Saranagati eNewsletter, November 2012, 'Tirumoola Nayanar', freely adapted from the Periapuranam and Siva Bhakta Vilasam. Asanas: Tirumantiram, Tantra 3, verses 558-563, tr. B. Natarajan (Himalayan Academy). Dating: S. Vaiyapuripillai, History of Tamil Language and Literature (1956; reprint 1988), p. 78 n. 1, as cited by Wikipedia. T. N. Ramachandran's English Periya Puranam (Tamil University, Thanjavur, 1990-1995) was not opened.
kept.evidence: Opened the Ramanasramam page. It says he reached 'Aaduthurai' (Tiruvavaduthurai), spent his days 'beneath the temple peepal tree', and then 'resumed his samadhi beneath the peepal tree, emerging ever so often to [write] a single verse in Tamil, one per year, over the next 3,000 years ... These 3,000 verses make up the Tirumantram.' It is credited to the November 2012 Saranagati eNewsletter, not a series title as the draft said. tamil.wiki quotes the Periya Puranam lines 'ஓர் ஆண்டுக்கு ஒன்று ஆக' (one for each year) and 'மன்னிய மூவாயிரத்து ஆண்டு இப்புவிமேல்' (three thousand years on this earth), plus the pipal tree near the temple, so the core is in Sekkizhar. Wikipedia (Tirumular) reports Vaiyapuripillai's early 8th century CE date. Opened Himalayan Academy Tantra 3 for verses 558-563 as quoted. shaivam.org (Ramachandran) returned 403, so I did not check his wording.
kept.safety: Passes after the frame is cut. The full legend has the yogi enter the body of a cowherd who had just died, with grieving cows and the cowherd's upset wife. That is a death, so leave it all out. Call 3,000 years a legend, not history. Do not repeat Tirumantiram 569-570, which say breath control makes an old body 'young and crystal-hard' and that 'the body then will perish not'. Those are overstated health claims.
kept.joke_angle: Use skeleton 10, 'Good news, bad news': 'Good news: I am as consistent as Tirumular. Bad news: at his speed, my hamstrings open in the year 5026.' The target is Boonchu's slow forward bend, not the saint or his verses.

kept.title: Gorakhnath, the teacher who shows up in every age
kept.story: A belief recorded by G. W. Briggs in 1938: in many places, Gorakhnath is seen as a teacher 'outside of the ordinary laws of time'. It is said he appeared on earth in each of the four world-ages, in a different place each time. Briggs read this as his followers linking their far-apart centres to one teacher.
kept.asana: Added, because the draft had none. It is the same loose link as the dung-heap story: HYP 1.57 (Sinh) says expert yogis call Bhadrasana 'Goraksa asana'. The nearest Ashtanga shape is Baddha Konasana, Primary series. It works best as the closing tag of the dung-heap Reel, so the video keeps one story.
kept.source: G. W. Briggs, Gorakhnath and the Kanphata Yogis (Calcutta: Y.M.C.A. Publishing House; London: Humphrey Milford, Oxford University Press, 1938), pp. 228-229 (Chapter 11, 'Gorakhnath'). Asana link: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 1.57, tr. Pancham Sinh.
kept.evidence: Opened the full Briggs text, pp. 228-229: 'in many places Gorakhnath is looked upon as more than a human teacher, outside of the ordinary laws of time, who has appeared on the earth in different ages (yuga). He is said to have lived in the Panjab at Peshawar, beyond Lahore, in the Satya (Krta) Yuga; at Gorakhpur in the Treta Yuga; at Hurmuj, beyond Dwaraka, in the Dvapara Yuga; and three months journey west of Gorakhpur, at Gorakhmari (Gorakhmandi) in Kathiawar in the Kali Yuga. This is evidently an attempt not only to refer the origin of the sect to the distant past, but to incorporate in the record references to widely separated places where Gorakhnath and his followers had headquarters and were well known.' The draft's quote, places and reading are correct. I did not open David Gordon White's The Alchemical Body.
kept.safety: Passes as belief, not fact. I cut the place list (Peshawar, Hurmuj, which is Hormuz) so the Reel does not drift into present-day borders or news. Also leave out the creation story on p. 228, where Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva become Gorakhnath's first disciples, because it ranks gods and could upset viewers. No health claims. Do not present kaya siddhi (a body that never ages) as something practice gives.
kept.joke_angle: Use skeleton 15, 'The understatement', with a tag: 'Gorakhnath showed up in all four world-ages. I show up before six, six mornings a week. One of us is a legend. The other one is just early.' The joke is on Boonchu's alarm clock, not on Gorakhnath.

kept.title: Six months upside down: no wrinkles, no grey hair?
kept.story: An old promise: the Hatha Yoga Pradipika says after six months of Viparita Karani, head down and feet up, 'the wrinkles and grey hair are not seen'. A 2021 Columbia study of 14 people saw some grey hairs regain colour as stress fell. It did not test yoga, and its senior author doubts long-grey hair turns dark again.
kept.asana: Confirmed. Viparita Karani is a mudra in HYP 3.78-81 (Sinh). 3.80: 'Place the head on the ground and the feet up into the sky, for a second only the first day, and increase this time daily.' The nearest Ashtanga forms are Salamba Sarvangasana and Sirsasana in the finishing sequence (ashtangayoga.info finishing list).
kept.source: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 3.78-81 (grey-hair line 3.81), tr. Pancham Sinh (Allahabad: Panini Office; usually cited as 1914); numbering varies by edition. Rosenberg A. M., Rausser S., ... Picard M., 'Quantitative mapping of human hair greying and reversal in relation to life stress', eLife 10:e67437 (2021). Columbia University Irving Medical Center news release, 22 June 2021, senior author Martin Picard.
kept.evidence: Sinh scan: 3.80 as quoted. 3.81: 'After six months, the wrinkles and grey hair are not seen. He who practises it daily, even for two hours, conquers death.' 3.79: 'If the food be scanty, it will burn him at once.' 3.29: Maha Vedha 'destroys old age, grey hair, and shaking of the body'. eLife full text (Europe PMC): 14 people (7 women, 7 men), mean age 35, range 9 to 65, 397 hairs; reversal 'coincided closely with the decline in stress' after a 2-week vacation. Columbia release (22 June 2021): '14 volunteers'; 'five hairs on that person's head reverted back to dark during the vacation'; Picard: 'we don't think that reducing stress in a 70-year-old who's been gray for years will darken their hair', and that stress matters most in middle age, near a greying threshold. The draft is accurate, but it needed to say the study did not test yoga or inversions.
kept.safety: Passes only as 'old promise, modern evidence', said with respect, not as fraud. Never say inversions reverse grey hair or wrinkles. The study did not test yoga, was small (14 people, mean age 35) and only shows hair changing alongside stress. Leave out 3.81's 'conquers death' and 3.79's food warning. Sirsasana and Sarvangasana put load on the neck, so add 'learn them from a teacher' and never suggest holding them longer for looks.
kept.joke_angle: Use skeleton 10, 'Good news, bad news': 'The old book says six months upside down and no grey hair. Science says the cure is a holiday. I run a shala six mornings a week. My hair has made its choice.' Use it only if Boonchu really has grey hairs, because the floor says true only.

kept.title: Pengzu: 800 years of daoyin
kept.story: The story goes that Pengzu, an official in ancient China, lived more than 800 years, from the Xia dynasty to the end of the Shang. An old book of immortals says he often ate a fine fungus called zhi and was 'good at daoyin and moving qi': guided stretching and breathing. His name became China's word for long life.
kept.asana: None. The theme is breath and daily practice. There is no historical link to any Ashtanga asana, so do not invent one.
kept.source: Liexian zhuan (Biographies of Exemplary Immortals), attributed to Liu Xiang (1st c. BCE), entry 'Pengzu': 彭祖者，殷大夫也 ... 歷夏至殷末八百餘歲。常食佳芝，善導引行氣. French tr. Max Kaltenmark, Le Lie-sien tchouan (Peking, 1953). Chinese text: Project Gutenberg eBook #25414.
kept.evidence: Downloaded the Gutenberg plain text (pg25414.txt). The Pengzu entry (lines 204-211) reads: 彭祖者，殷大夫也。姓籛名鏗，帝顓頊之孫陸終氏之中子，歷夏至殷末八百餘歲。常食佳芝，善導引行氣. So: an official (大夫) of the Yin/Shang, lived from the Xia to the end of the Yin, over 800 years, often ate fine zhi, good at daoyin and moving qi. All facts in the retelling match. The ancestry line (descendant of the ruler Zhuanxu) is left out. The variant readings in the notes (桂芝; 700 in Li Shan) were not re-checked, so the retelling cites the Liexian zhuan only and says 'more than 800'.
kept.safety: Labelled as a story. No royalty (ancestry left out), no conflict, no violence. Health: 800 years is legend, not a claim; do not suggest that zhi fungus or daoyin extends life, and do not recommend zhi as a supplement.
kept.joke_angle: Pengzu practised daoyin for 800 years. I've practised Ashtanga for 20, and at 5 a.m. my hamstrings already feel like his.

kept.title: Zhuangzi and the bear-hang crowd
kept.story: Zhuangzi, chapter 15, describes people who breathe out the old and in the new, hang like a bear and stretch like a bird, hoping to live as long as Pengzu. Then it says the sage reaches long life without these exercises, through calm and stillness. A silk chart buried in 168 BCE labels one figure 'bear hang'.
kept.asana: No direct asana. Loose echo only, no historical link: bird-named asanas such as Kukkutasana (Primary Series) and Bakasana (Intermediate Series).
kept.source: Zhuangzi ch. 15 'Keyi' (Kho I, 'Ingrained Ideas'), tr. James Legge, The Texts of Taoism Part I, Sacred Books of the East vol. 39 (Oxford, 1891), p. 364: 'Blowing and breathing with open mouth; inhaling and exhaling the breath; expelling the old breath and taking in new; passing their time like the (dormant) bear, and stretching and twisting (the neck) like a bird ... wish to live as long as Pang Zu' and '... who attain to longevity without the management (of the breath) ... whose placidity is unlimited'. Chinese: 吹呴呼吸，吐故納新，熊經鳥申，為壽而已矣 ... 不導引而壽 (zh.wikisource 莊子/刻意). Also H. A. Giles, Chuang Tzu (1889), 'stretching like a bear and craning like a bird' (Gutenberg #59709). Chart: Daoyin tu, Mawangdui Tomb 3, Changsha (sealed 168 BCE, excavated 1973), 44 figures, 31 captions survive; figure 41 is captioned 熊經 (bear hang). Figure 32's caption reads only 信 (伸, 'stretch'); the 'bird' is a modern scholarly restoration.
kept.evidence: sacred-texts.com is behind a Cloudflare block (403), so I checked Legge in the archive.org scan of SBE vol. 39 instead. Page 364 has the quoted wording word for word ('Pang 3w' in the OCR = Päng Zû), plus Legge's footnote that the text literally says 'Bear-passing, bird-stretching'. It also has 'who attain to longevity without the management (of the breath)', which supports the sage line. Chinese text checked on zh.wikisource (莊子/刻意): 熊經鳥申 ... 不導引而壽 ... 澹然无極. Giles 1889 on Gutenberg agrees. Chart: the Anhui University of Chinese Medicine page (ahtcm.edu.cn) says 原图32「信（伸)」和原图41「熊经」 match the Zhuangzi line and lists '(鸟)信（伸）', so the bird caption is restored, not written. Chinajiandu.cn: 44 figures, 31 surviving captions. Wikipedia and the Wellcome Collection: Tomb 3, 168 BC, found 1973. I could not open the Hunan Museum pages (503 and connection reset). Fix: the claim that the chart 'labels the same two moves' is overstated, so the retelling now says it labels one figure 'bear hang'. The Burton Watson wording was not checked and is not cited.
kept.safety: No conflict, violence or royalty. Zhuangzi is gently contrasting stretchers with the sage, not mocking them, so do not frame it as 'Zhuangzi mocks yogis' and do not use it to knock the Ashtanga method. No health claims. The Kukkutasana and Bakasana link is an analogy only and must be presented that way. Avoid the earlier 'gave one of them a Mysore room' joke, because it can read as a dig at the practice.
kept.joke_angle: Zhuangzi says the sage lives long through calm, not stretching. I've done twenty years of the stretching at 5 a.m., and I'm still waiting for the calm. Apparently it doesn't do early mornings.

kept.title: Hua Tuo: a door hinge never rots
kept.story: Hua Tuo, a doctor, told his student Wu Pu that the body wants work, but never to the extreme. Moving keeps the blood flowing, 'like a door hinge that never rots'. He taught the Five Animal Frolics: tiger, deer, bear, ape and bird. An old history records that Wu Pu, past ninety, had sharp ears and eyes and firm teeth.
kept.asana: No single asana. Loose echo only, no historical link: the bird frolic and bird-named asanas such as Kukkutasana (Primary Series) and Bakasana (Intermediate Series). AshtangaYoga.info series sheets confirm both placements.
kept.source: Chen Shou, Sanguozhi (Records of the Three Kingdoms, late 3rd c. CE), juan 29 (Wei shu), biography of Hua Tuo: 人體欲得勞動，但不當使極爾。動搖則谷氣得消，血脈流通，病不得生，譬猶戶樞不朽是也 ... 吾有一術，名五禽之戲，一曰虎，二曰鹿，三曰熊，四曰猿，五曰鳥 ... 普施行之，年九十餘，耳目聰明，齒牙完堅. Parallel in Hou Hanshu 82B; English in Kenneth DeWoskin, Doctors, Diviners, and Magicians of Ancient China (Columbia UP, 1983). The older hinge proverb is in Lüshi Chunqiu 3.2 'Jin shu' (c. 239 BCE): 流水不腐，戶樞不螻，動也, tr. Knoblock and Riegel, The Annals of Lü Buwei (Stanford UP, 2000).
kept.evidence: Downloaded Sanguozhi juan 29 from zh.wikisource. The passage matches exactly: the body wants work but not to the extreme (不當使極); movement lets the blood flow (血脈流通) 'like a door hinge that does not rot' (戶樞不朽); the five animals are 虎 tiger, 鹿 deer, 熊 bear, 猿 ape, 鳥 bird; Wu Pu, past ninety (年九十餘), had sharp hearing and sight (耳目聰明) and complete, firm teeth (齒牙完堅). The sweat-and-powder detail (沾濡汗出，因上著粉) and 熊頸鴟顧 are also there. Checked Lüshi Chunqiu book 3, 盡數, on zh.wikisource: 流水不腐，戶樞不螻，動也. AshtangaYoga.info Primary Series PDF lists KUKKUTASANA (after Garbha Pindasana), and the Intermediate Series PDF lists BAKASANA A.
kept.safety: Leave out Hua Tuo's later fate, and the surgery and cold-water treatments in the same juan. 'Movement keeps the blood flowing' is quoted as an ancient doctor's words, not a medical claim. Wu Pu reaching ninety is a historical record, not proof that the frolics or Ashtanga extend life, and the line that 'illness cannot arise' (病不得生) is deliberately left out. 'Never to the extreme' (不當使極) sits well with safe Ashtanga practice.
kept.joke_angle: Hua Tuo said: work the body, but never to the extreme. My hamstrings have followed this advice faithfully for 20 years.

kept.title: Zhang Guo and the folding donkey
kept.story: The story goes that Zhang Guo, later counted among the Eight Immortals, rode a white donkey that went tens of thousands of li (Chinese miles) a day. At rest he folded it thin as paper into a box; to ride, he sprayed it with water. Elders said in their childhood he already claimed to be several hundred years old.
kept.asana: None. There is no asana link; use it only for the theme of age and how students see their teacher.
kept.source: Taiping guangji (compiled 977-978), juan 30 'Zhang Guo', citing Minghuang zalu, Xuanshi zhi and Xu shenxian zhuan (出《明皇雜錄》、《宣室志》、《續神仙傳》): 耆老云：「為兒童時見之，自言數百歲矣。」... 果常乘一白驢，日行數萬里，休則重疊之，其厚如紙，置於巾箱中；乘則以水噀之，還成驢矣. Eight Immortals and later art: Princeton University Art Museum, Wang Yuanxun (1728-1807), 'Zhang Guolao Riding on a Donkey', object 22846: 'One of the Daoist Eight Immortals ... often represented facing backward while riding a white donkey ... folded up like a piece of paper for storage'.
kept.evidence: Downloaded Taiping guangji juan 30 from zh.wikisource. The quoted lines match exactly: the elders saw him as children and he said he was several hundred years old; a white donkey covering several tens of thousands of li a day; folded as thin as paper into a 巾箱 box; sprayed with water (噀) to become a donkey again. The entry closes by citing three works, 明皇雜錄, 宣室志 and 續神仙傳, but the item named only two, so the source line is fixed. The Princeton record (data.artmuseum.princeton.edu/objects/22846) confirms the 'Daoist Eight Immortals' label, the backward riding and the paper folding. Note that Princeton gives 'a thousand miles a day', so follow the Chinese text for the distance. The story was trimmed to under 60 words and 'li' is glossed for non-native readers.
kept.safety: The full source entry includes emperors summoning him, a staged death, him knocking out his own teeth with blood, and a Daoist struck down bleeding. None of this goes in the retelling. Do not explain the backward riding (no early source). He is a revered Daoist immortal, so the joke stays on Boonchu, not on Zhang Guo or his donkey. No health claims.
kept.joke_angle: Elders said that as children they already heard him claim to be several hundred years old. My new students in Bangkok look at me the same way, and I only admit to 53.

kept.title: 'Seventy is rare' sits next to a wine debt
kept.story: Chinese people call age 70 'guxi', meaning 'rare since ancient times'. It comes from a spring poem by Du Fu, written in 758: 'I have wine debts everywhere I go; since ancient times, few live to seventy.' The poem means: enjoy spring now. It was never a health fact. China's average life expectancy reached 79.25 years in 2025.
kept.source: Du Fu, 'Qujiang' (Winding River), poem 2 of 2, spring 758 CE (Qianyuan 1): 酒債尋常行處有，人生七十古來稀 (Chinese Wikisource 曲江二首; English is a plain rendering of the Chinese). Number: National Health Commission of China, 2025 Statistical Bulletin on Health Development (released 28 Aug 2026): life expectancy 79.25 at end of 2025. Earlier figure: NHC English site, 10 March 2025, 79 years in 2024.
kept.evidence: Opened zh.wikisource 曲江二首: the couplet 酒債尋常行處有，人生七十古來稀 is in poem 2 (其二), lines 3-4, right after 朝回日日典春衣，每向江頭盡醉歸 (pawning spring clothes to drink by the river); the poem ends 暫時相賞莫相違 (enjoy it while it lasts), so the carpe diem reading holds. Date 758 spring confirmed by cn-poetry.com and matches Du Fu's time as Reminder in Chang'an. Opened en.nhc.gov.cn (10 Mar 2025): 'reached 79 years in 2024', '+0.4 years from 2023' (so 78.6 in 2023 is correct). FIX 1: a newer official figure exists. Science and Technology Daily (28 Aug 2026) quotes the NHC 2025 bulletin: 2025年末，我国人均预期寿命达到79.25岁. Story updated to 79.25 (2025). FIX 2: could not open Stephen Owen's text for this poem, so his wording is unverified; removed the 'tr. Owen' attribution and used a plain translation of the Chinese instead.
kept.safety: Safe. No war, politics or royalty in the retelling (left out that Du Fu was out of favour at court). Du Fu is not mocked. Mild alcohol mention ('wine debts'); fine for adults, but swap to 'debts at every wine shop' or drop the line if the account avoids drink references. The 79.25 figure is a national average, not a yoga claim: do not imply practice adds years.
kept.joke_angle: Du Fu said seventy is rare. I am 53, twenty years of Ashtanga, up at 4 a.m. every day. Seventy, maybe. My toes in Paschimottanasana? Also rare. I see them about twice a week.

kept.title: Tithonus: long life, no youth
kept.story: In a Greek myth, the dawn goddess Eos loved a man named Tithonus. She asked Zeus to let him live forever, but she did not think to ask for youth. He grew so old he 'could not move nor lift his limbs'. She laid him in a room behind shining doors. Later tellings turn him into a cicada.
kept.source: Homeric Hymn 5, To Aphrodite, lines 218-238, tr. Hugh G. Evelyn-White, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns and Homerica (Loeb, 1914), Perseus Digital Library. Cicada ending: later tradition, e.g. Hieronymus of Rhodes (3rd c. BCE) and Robin Hard, Routledge Handbook of Greek Mythology p. 47, as cited in Wikipedia 'Tithonus'; Britannica 'Tithonus' also gives the cicada as a later version.
kept.evidence: Opened Perseus, Evelyn-White 1914: lines 222-224 'Too simple was queenly Eos: she thought not in her heart to ask youth for him'; 231-234 'when loathsome old age pressed full upon him, and he could not move nor lift his limbs'; 234-235 'she laid him in a room and put to the shining doors'; 235-237 'There he babbles endlessly, and no more has strength at all, such as once he had in his supple limbs.' Zeus ('Son of Cronos') grants deathlessness. All quotes in the draft match. FIX: the draft cited Tzetzes, Chiliades book 8 for the cicada; I could not confirm that citation (Britannica page returned 403; Wikipedia cites Tzetzes only for an etymology). Replaced with sources I could see: Wikipedia 'Tithonus' ('In later tellings, he eventually became a cicada', citing Hard p. 47 and the Suda; Hieronymus of Rhodes version) and a search summary of Britannica ('in a later version Tithonus was transformed into a cicada'). Also changed 'she forgot' to 'she did not think to', which is closer to the hymn and gentler toward the goddess. No asana claimed, so nothing to check there.
kept.safety: Safe. Royal titles left out (hymn calls Eos 'queenly'; Tithonus is a Trojan prince elsewhere). No death, no curse. Goddess and Zeus named neutrally; nothing mocks them. No health claim: use 'Long life was never the gift; moving was' as a reflection, not as 'yoga keeps you young'.
kept.joke_angle: Tithonus 'could not move nor lift his limbs.' I read that and thought: someone has filmed me at 5 a.m., before the first Surya Namaskar. Twenty years of practice, and my hamstrings still wake up an hour after I do.

kept.title: Urashima: don't open the box
kept.story: This Japanese legend is over 1,300 years old. A fisherman named Urashima meets a turtle and is taken to a palace under the sea. After a short stay he goes home, but 300 years have passed. He opens a box he was told never to open. White smoke rises, and he becomes an old man.
kept.asana: Kurmasana (turtle) and Supta Kurmasana, Ashtanga Primary Series
kept.source: JAANUS (Japanese Architecture and Art Net Users System, Columbia University), entry 'Urashima 浦島': oldest extant version in the Tango fudoki (713); undersea palace (Ryuugu); turtle rescued or caught in some versions; absent 300 years; box never to be opened; white smoke; becomes an old man. Also Man'yoshu book 9, poems 1740-1741, 'Mizunoe no Urashimako', by Takahashi no Mushimaro (8th c.). Asana: AshtangaYoga.info Primary Series list.
kept.evidence: Opened JAANUS: 'The oldest extant version is found in the Tango fudoki (Local Records of Tango; 713)'; the woman's original form is a sea turtle, 'rescued by him from malicious children' or caught by him; taken to the 'fabulous undersea palace' Ryuugu; 'he had been absent for 300 years'; box with a warning never to open it; 'wisps of white smoke'; he becomes 'a wizened old man and dies'. JAANUS does not mention the Man'yoshu; confirmed separately by search (asahi-net Takahashi no Mushimaro page and Japanese university papers: Man'yoshu 9-1740/1741 詠水江浦嶋子). Asana: opened ashtangayoga.info Primary Series page: Kurmasana is no. 25 and Supta Kurmasana no. 26 of 41. Story matches the source; I only simplified wording, said 'meets a turtle' (covers both rescued and caught versions), and added the 713 date as 'over 1,300 years old'.
kept.safety: Safe as written. Stops at 'old man': the source says he then dies, so do not continue the story. Otohime is 'daughter of the Dragon King' in JAANUS: royal title left out. Left out the 'malicious children' detail. Do not present the smoke box as a lesson about ageing and health; it is a legend.
kept.joke_angle: Urashima spent a few days under the sea and came home 300 years older. I did my first full Intermediate Series at 53 and looked in the mirror after. Same story, no turtle.

kept.title: Crane 1,000 years, turtle 10,000
kept.story: Japanese people say 'the crane lives 1,000 years, the turtle 10,000'. The crane part comes from the Chinese book Huainanzi. The turtle part may have been added in Japan. In the old Otogizoshi storybook version, Urashima does not stay old. He becomes a crane. He and the sea woman, who was the turtle, are honoured together as gods.
kept.asana: Bakasana A and B (crane), Ashtanga Intermediate Series; Kurmasana and Supta Kurmasana (turtle), Ashtanga Primary Series
kept.source: Huainanzi ch. 17 'Shuolin xun' (c. 139 BCE): 鶴壽千歲，以極其游 (Chinese Wikisource 淮南子/說林訓). Mainichi Shimbun Kotoba Salon, Kouetsu Center (16 and 27 Sept 2015), citing the Iwanami Kotowaza Jiten: 亀は万年 'may have been added later in Japan'. National Diet Library, 'Hon no Mangekyo no. 36', ch. 2 (Otogizoshi vol. 21, Urashima Taro). Dating and 'married pair of myojin': Digital Daijisen via Kotobank. Asanas: AshtangaYoga.info Primary list and Intermediate (Nadi Shodana) vinyasa PDF.
kept.evidence: Opened Wikisource 淮南子/說林訓: '鶴壽千歲，以極其游；蜉蝣朝生而暮死，而盡其樂' (crane lives 1,000 years to roam fully; the mayfly lives one day and enjoys it fully; a nice extra line for the caption). Opened Mainichi Kotoba Salon: 「亀は万年」は「のちに日本で補われたものかもしれない」 (Iwanami; hedged, so 'may' is right). Opened NDL: 「最後は鶴になり、亀であった乙姫と共に神様として祀られるエンディング」. Kotobank: Digital Daijisen 「浦島が老翁となったあと鶴と化し、乙姫が化した亀と夫婦の明神になる」; Muromachi dating is hedged in dictionaries (室町時代の成立か), so I left 'Muromachi' out of the story. Asanas: ashtangayoga.info Primary list has Kurmasana (25) and Supta Kurmasana (26); its Intermediate Series PDF lists BAKASANA A and BAKASANA B after Supta Vajrasana. All claims confirmed.
kept.safety: Safe. Being honoured as gods (myojin at a Shinto shrine) is told respectfully, no conflict. Otohime's princess title left out ('sea woman').
