The proverb is a blessing, not a health claim: do not say cranes, turtles or these asanas add years. The mayfly line mentions dying at dusk; it is an insect, no victims, but optional.
kept.joke_angle: The crane lives a thousand years, the turtle ten thousand. In Bakasana I am a crane for about four seconds. In Supta Kurmasana, with my hamstrings, I am a turtle for ten thousand years, because I cannot get out.

kept.title: Ilya Muromets gets up
kept.story: In a Russian folk tale, Ilya of Murom could not use his arms or legs for thirty years. Two wandering pilgrims asked him to fetch a cup from the cellar. He lifted an arm, stretched a leg and stood. After one cup he said he could turn the earth over. Too much, they said, and a second cup halved it.
kept.asana: Utthita Hasta Padangusthasana (Primary Series standing sequence: stand, lift and stretch one leg). This is a thematic link only; the tale names no asana.
kept.source: Matvei M. Korguev (1883-1943), 'Ilya Muromets', prose folk tale (skazka), 1939, Russian Wikisource (page marked 'unverified', transcribed from litena.ru). Thirty years also in Brockhaus-Efron Encyclopaedic Dictionary, vol. IV (1891), article 'Bogatyri', pp. 147-157. English: 'The Cure of Ilya Muromets', in James Bailey and Tatyana Ivanova, An Anthology of Russian Folk Epics (M. E. Sharpe, 1998). Asana list: AshtangaYoga.info, Primary Series (Yoga Chikitsa).
kept.evidence: Opened the Korguev text. It says 'И пролёжал Илья ровно тридцать лет': thirty years, not 33. The visitors are 'калики перехожие' (two wandering pilgrims). They ask him to bring 'пива эту чашку полную' from his father's cellar: a full cup of BEER. He raises an arm, stretches a leg and stands, then drinks it in one gulp. He says that if there were a pillar from earth to sky with a gold ring, he would grab it and turn over the whole earth. The pilgrims say 'Церез меру мы силы Илье дали, надо сбавить' (we gave too much strength, it must be reduced, or Mother Earth will not carry him). After a second small cup he has 'силушки во половинушку' (half strength). Corrections to the draft: (a) the pilgrims did not just 'tell him to rise', they asked him to fetch the cup; (b) 'turn the earth over' is conditional on the pillar and ring; (c) Korguev's text is a prose tale, not a sung epic; (d) the Wikisource page is flagged unverified. Brockhaus-Efron (opened on Wikisource, ESBE 'Богатыри', 1891): 'Илья сидит сиднем тридцать лет; получает силу от калик перехожих (по некоторым былинам, от Святогора)'. Bailey and Ivanova: confirmed the book (M. E. Sharpe, 1998). A secondary summary describes 'The Cure of Ilya Muromets' as thirty years paralysed, cured by passing pilgrims with a drink. I did not see the page itself. 'Thirty years and three' is a popular phrase and does not appear in Korguev. Asana: Utthita Hasta Padangusthasana A and B are listed in the Primary Series on AshtangaYoga.info.
kept.safety: Label it as a folk tale. Tell only the healing scene. The rest of Korguev's tale (Nightingale the Robber, fights, the prince in Kyiv) has violence and royalty, so leave it out. In the text the pilgrims ask for alms 'for Christ's sake'. Keep them as 'wandering pilgrims' with no religious framing. The drink is beer, so say 'a cup' (accurate, and no alcohol on a yoga channel). Make no health claim: never suggest that practice cures paralysis. The asana link is the teacher's own theme, not part of the tale.
kept.joke_angle: Ilya's legs woke up after thirty years. My hamstrings are on year twenty of Ashtanga, so in Utthita Hasta Padangusthasana I still have ten years to go before I reach my toe.

kept.title: Ruesi dat ton: hermits who stretched
kept.story: Thai tradition says hermits (ruesi), stiff after long meditation, stretched to ease their aches. This is ruesi dat ton: 'the hermit bends his own body'. In 1836, craftsmen at Wat Pho in Bangkok cast hermit statues in 80 postures from a zinc and tin alloy, each with a four-line verse on stone about what it was meant to help.
kept.asana: No single asana. It is Thailand's own cousin of asana practice (one art historian says it likely drew on Indian yoga ideas, adapted to Thai art).
kept.source: MGR Online, 'ยืดเส้นยืดสายด้วย "ฤาษีดัดตน" ภูมิปัญญากายบริหารแบบไทยๆ', 23 April 2009. Orawan Chueanoi (อรวรรณ เชื้อน้อย; the draft spelled it 'Chuennoi'), 'Ruesi Sculpture at Phra Chetuphon Wimon Mangalaram Temple: Art Forms in the Early Rattanakosin Period', Journal of Chandrakasemsarn 27(1), Jan-Jun 2021, pp. 75-88. Wat Pho inscriptions: UNESCO Memory of the World, 2011, 1,431 stone inscriptions made 1831-1841.
kept.evidence: MGR Online (opened): 'ท่าทางต่างๆ ของฤาษีดัดตนเป็นการฝึกสมาธิบำเพ็ญเพียรของฤาษีในอดีต' and 'เมื่อฤาษีเกิดอาการเมื่อยขบก็ใช้วิธีการดัดตนบรรเทาอาการ'. It also gives 80 postures cast in 'สังกะสีผสมดีบุก เรียกว่า ชิน' and 'โคลงสี่สุภาพ 80 โคลง' on stone describing the benefits of each. It gives no exact year. Chueanoi 2021 (opened the PDF): Chula Sakarat 1198 = B.E. 2379 = 1836, statues in 80 postures. The total was 82 figures, because two postures show two hermits helping each other, so the draft's '80 statues' is wrong. Verses on all 80. A Samut Thai manuscript with drawings of all 80 was finished on 20 April 1838. Her survey found 28 postures (29 figures) at the temple today. Only 19 postures (20 figures) match the 1830s manuscript and are judged the oldest. The temple recast figures in 2008 to complete 80 again. So 'surviving' in the draft notes needs care, because today's set mixes old and new. Her conclusion: the statues likely drew on Indian yoga beliefs, adapted to Thai Buddhist art. MGR notes that a comparison study found the postures differ from Indian yoga, so 'cousin' fits better than 'copy'. UNESCO: 1,431 inscriptions, 1831-1841, registered 2011, confirmed. Salguero (jivaka.net) confirms inscriptions naming ailments such as sciatica. Verse metre: a khlong si suphap is a four-line form.
kept.safety: Every primary source names a king (Rama III ordered the casting; Rama I appears earlier) and princes who wrote verses. Leave all royalty out and say 'craftsmen'. Wat Pho is a Buddhist temple, so do not joke about the hermits, monks or temple. Do not list ailments or say the stretches cure anything. 'What it was meant to help' is a historical statement about the verses, not a medical claim. Present the origin as tradition ('Thai tradition says'), because sources date the practice only to the late 1700s and say older origins are 'believed'.
kept.joke_angle: Bangkok has had a stretching manual cast in metal since 1836, made for stiff hermits. I am a stiff Bangkok teacher with twenty years of practice, and my hamstrings are still on verse one.

kept.title: Ponce de León never looked for it
kept.story: Many people learn that the Spanish explorer Juan Ponce de León sailed to Florida in 1513 to find the Fountain of Youth. Historians say no paper from his lifetime links him to a fountain. His contracts talk about finding new islands. The chronicler Oviedo first tied him to it in 1535, twenty-two years after the voyage.
kept.asana: None. The source has no asana link. Do not attach one as an 'anti-ageing' asana.
kept.source: Jesse Greenspan, 'The Myth of Ponce de León and the Fountain of Youth', History.com, 2 April 2013 (updated 3 September 2026). Matthew Shaer, 'Ponce De Leon Never Searched for the Fountain of Youth', Smithsonian Magazine, June 2013 (historian J. Michael Francis, University of South Florida St. Petersburg). Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo, Historia general y natural de las Indias, part one printed 1535. Earlier fountain mention without Ponce: Peter Martyr, Decades, Decade II, ch. X (printed 1516).
kept.evidence: History.com (opened): sailed March 1513; 'Nowhere in either this contract or a follow-up contract was the Fountain of Youth mentioned'; Francis: 'What Ponce is really looking for is islands that will become part of what he hopes will be a profitable new governorship'. It says Oviedo in 1535 accused Ponce of seeking the fountain. Smithsonian (opened): Francis 'says no mention of a Fountain of Youth occurs in any known documents from Ponce's lifetime', and Ponce's name 'wasn't tied to the Fountain of Youth until 14 years after his death'. Correction: the draft line 'No known document from his lifetime mentions a fountain' is too broad. Peter Martyr's Decades (Decade II, ch. X, printed 1516, while Ponce was alive) already mention a spring that makes old men young, on an island called Boyuca or Ananeo. Martyr does not name Ponce (Wikipedia 'Fountain of Youth'; Acción Cultural Española 'La Florida' exhibition page). So the safe claim is that nothing from his lifetime LINKS HIM to a fountain, and his own writings never mention one. I dropped 'letters talk about land' because I found no source quoting his letters. I also dropped 'schoolbooks', which no source states. Cranach note: 'The Fountain of Youth' is dated 1546 and hangs in the Gemäldegalerie Berlin (confirmed). Inv. 593 appears only as a reference code (DE_smbGG_593), so it is not firmly confirmed.
kept.safety: Ponce de León was a conquistador. His real life includes the conquest of Puerto Rico, a royal contract from the Spanish king, and his death in 1521 from a wound in a fight. Keep all of this out. That is why the story says 'twenty-two years after the voyage' and not 'after he died'. Skip Oviedo's insults about Ponce's motives. Health: do not say daily practice is a literal fountain of youth or reverses ageing; keep it as a joke about habit. Cranach's painting shows nude bathers, which may break Instagram and Chinese platform rules, so crop it or choose another image.
kept.joke_angle: Ponce de León never searched for the Fountain of Youth. I have, for twenty years. It opens before sunrise in Bangkok, it is mostly my own sweat, and at 53 I am still waiting for results.

kept.title: Six months upside down: no wrinkles, no grey hair
kept.story: The Hatha Yoga Pradipika promises: turn upside down, head on the ground and feet up, a little longer each day, and after six months wrinkles and grey hair are not seen. No study has tested this. In a Columbia University study of 14 people, a few grey hairs regained colour when stress dropped, once after a holiday.
kept.asana: Salamba Sarvangasana and Sirsasana, the upside-down asanas of the Ashtanga Finishing Sequence (Yoga Mala asanas 32 and 39). The text's Viparita Karani is a mudra, not an Ashtanga asana, but in Yoga Mala's Sirsasana section Jois quotes the same 'yama matram' line ('we can dwell in Shirshasana for three hours') and says to build up 5 minutes at a time.
kept.source: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 3.79-3.82 (Sanskrit numbering on sacred-texts; Pancham Sinh's English labels 3.78-3.81), tr. Pancham Sinh, Sacred Books of the Hindus vol. XV pt. III, Panini Office, Allahabad, 1914 (scan dated January 1915). Sinh 3.80: 'Place the head on the ground and the feet up into the sky, for a second only the first day, and increase this time daily.' Sinh 3.81: 'After six months, the wrinkles and grey hair are not seen. He who practises it daily, even for two hours, conquers death.' Swami Muktibodhananda (Bihar School of Yoga), verse 3.82: 'After six months of practice, grey hairs and wrinkles become inconspicuous. One who practices it for yama (three hours) conquers death.' Evidence: Rosenberg AM et al., eLife 2021;10:e67437 (Columbia University Irving Medical Center).
kept.evidence: sacred-texts.com refused my fetcher (403), so I read a copy of the same Sinh chapter III page already saved in this session, then checked it against the 1915 Digital Library of India scan and Muktibodhananda's book on archive.org. The verse wording and numbering in the item are exact: Sanskrit 82 'valitam palitam caiva sanmasordhvam na drsyate / yama-matram tu yo nityam abhyaset sa tu kalajit'. Sinh says 'two hours' and Muktibodhananda says 'yama (three hours)'. Sinh 3.76 has the moon nectar 'devoured by the Surya'. Gheranda Samhita 3.33-36 (Vasu) and Shiva Samhita 4.45-46 (Vasu 1914, 'daily for three hours, conquers death') match the item notes. Rosenberg full text (PMC8219384): 397 hairs from 14 healthy donors (7 women, 7 men, ages 9-65), recruited over 2.5 years 'indicative of the rarity'. Reversal was seen only in people aged 9-39. In one person, reversal 'coincided closely with the decline in stress... following a 2-week vacation'. The model suggests reversal is temporary and only for hairs near the greying threshold. No study of inversions on hair or wrinkles exists. Alam 2018 (JAMA Dermatol 154:365, Northwestern news page): 27 women aged 40-65 recruited, 16 completed; estimated age went 50.8 to 49.6 (week 8) to 48.1 (week 20). It was facial exercise, not inversions, with no control group, and the regimen's founder (Happy Face Yoga) was a co-author. I left it out of the story because it is not about inversions.
kept.safety: Safe after the fix: no violence, royalty or conflict; I dropped 'conquers death' from the retelling. The health claim is labelled as the text's promise and corrected with the study. Do not suggest long holds: Muktibodhananda's own commentary says not to practise for three hours because 'the body will be unable to cope', and that elderly people should not start inversions late in life because of stroke risk. Add a line that inversions are learned step by step with a teacher, and are not for people with neck injury, uncontrolled high blood pressure or eye pressure problems unless a doctor agrees. Never present inversions as anti-ageing.
kept.joke_angle: Twenty years upside down every morning, and Boonchu's grey hair still arrives right on schedule. In the Columbia study, colour came back after a holiday, so his best anti-ageing plan may be a week off, not a longer headstand.

kept.title: 'Too old after forty': Guruji's answer
kept.story: Some said yoga, even Sirsasana, is not for anyone over forty. In Yoga Mala, Pattabhi Jois answered: 'not borne out by experience'. Young, old, very old, sick or weak: all can practise, except the lazy. 'Old' meant over sixty; 'very old', over ninety. At Tufts, nine people aged about 90 gained 174% strength in eight weeks of weight training.
kept.asana: Sirsasana (Ashtanga Finishing Sequence). The passage is in Yoga Mala's Shirshasana section (asana 39), just before Baddha Padmasana (40). It is not in the Baddha Padmasana/Yoga Mudra section, as the item said.
kept.source: Sri K. Pattabhi Jois, Yoga Mala (Kannada 1962; English tr. Eddie Stern, 1999; North Point Press 2002/2010), section 39 Shirshasana: 'Claims are also made that Shirshasana or yoga of any kind should not be practiced by people after they have reached the age of forty. This is not borne out by experience or by the shastrakaras.' ... 'whether one is young or old ("old" here meaning above sixty years of age, and "very old," beyond ninety)... anyone... can practice yoga, except those who are lazy.' He quotes Hatha Yoga Pradipika 1.64 ('Yuva vrddho'tivrddho va...'; Sinh 1914 labels it 1.66: 'Whether young, old or too old, sick or lean, one who discards laziness, gets success if he practises Yoga.'). Evidence: Fiatarone MA et al., JAMA 1990;263(22):3029-3034 (Tufts University).
kept.evidence: I read the English Yoga Mala text saved in this session. The quotes are exact, but they sit inside section '39. SHIRSHASANA' (TOC: 39 Shirshasana, 40 Baddha Padmasana). The 'YOGA MUDRA, BADDHA PADMASANA, 9TH VINYASA' line in the middle of the passage is only a photo caption, so the item's location was wrong. In Yoga Mala the HYP verse is rendered 'Whether young or old, or very old / sick or debilitated / one who is vigilant attains, by means of practice, success in all the yogas', and later cited as 'Hatha Yoga Pradipika i:64', with 'yoga is very important for anyone eight years or older'. In Sinh (sacred-texts copy) the verse is English label 66; Sinh 67 and 68 are 'by merely reading books' and 'particular dress (Vesa)', both confirmed. Fiatarone abstract (via NCBI E-utilities): 'Ten frail, institutionalized volunteers aged 90 +/- 1 years undertook 8 weeks of high-intensity resistance training... Strength gains averaged 174% +/- 31% in the 9 subjects who completed training. Midthigh muscle area increased 9.0%... tandem gait speed improved 48%', residents 'up to 96 years of age'. The abstract shows no control group.
kept.safety: Safe: no conflict, royalty or mockery, and Guruji is quoted with respect. The Tufts result is weight training in frail nursing-home residents, a small study of 10 people, not a yoga study. Present it as 'old bodies still answer training', never as proof that yoga or Sirsasana reverses ageing. Older beginners should learn Sirsasana gradually with a teacher.
kept.joke_angle: By Guruji's own definition, Boonchu at 53 is not even 'old' for another seven years, so his stiff hamstrings have officially lost their favourite excuse.

kept.title: The old man who becomes sixteen
kept.story: The Hatha Yoga Pradipika promises the bandhas restore youth: with Uddiyana, 'if old, becomes young again'; with Mula Bandha, 'even an old man becomes young'; one breath practice makes you 'as it were 16 years old'. Nobody turns sixteen. But at the Mayo Clinic, 12 weeks of interval training raised muscle energy capacity 69% in people aged 65 to 80.
kept.asana: Mula Bandha and Uddiyana Bandha, used throughout Ashtanga asana practice. Yoga Mala says the three bandhas 'should be performed while practicing asana'. 'Held through every asana' overstates it: Jois himself writes 'There is no mula bandha in this asana' for one Primary Series asana (Kukkutasana).
kept.source: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 2.47, 3.58 and 3.65 (Sanskrit numbering; Sinh labels the last two 3.57 and 3.64), tr. Pancham Sinh, 1914. 2.47: 'By pulling up the Apana Vayu and by forcing the Prana Vayu down the throat, the Yogi, liberated from old age, becomes young, as it were 16 years old.' 3.57: 'The practiser of this, if old, becomes young again.' 3.64: 'Even an old man becomes young by constantly practising Mula Bandha.' Muktibodhananda 2.47: 'the yogi becomes free from old age and appears as if sixteen years of age.' Evidence: Robinson MM et al. (Mayo Clinic), Cell Metabolism 2017;25(3):581-592.
kept.evidence: I used the saved sacred-texts copies (live site 403). Chapter II verse 47 is exact, with Sanskrit 'sodasabda-vaya bhavet'. In chapter III the Uddiyana verse is Sanskrit 58 ('vrddho'pi tarunayate') with English label 57. The Mula Bandha verse is English label 64 ('Even an old man becomes young...'). Muktibodhananda (archive.org) confirms 2.47. Robinson full text (PMC5423095): young 18-30 and older 65-80, 12 weeks of training. 'HIIT increased maximal absolute mitochondrial respiration in young (+49%) and older adults (+69%)', and 'RT did not increase mitochondrial respiration significantly in either age group'. The abstract says HIIT 'reversed many age-related differences in the proteome'. The ScienceDaily/Cell Press release gives '36 men and 36 women'. I also read Yoga Mala's bandha lines: 'they should be performed while practicing asana' and the Kukkutasana exception.
kept.safety: Safe after the fix: no violence or royalty, and I left out 'a lion for the elephant of death' (Sinh 3.56) and Jalandhara 'destroys old age and death' (3.69). The Mayo result comes from high-intensity cycling intervals in previously sedentary adults, not from bandhas. Do not imply that bandhas reverse ageing. 'Muscle energy capacity' means mitochondrial respiration, not looking younger.
kept.joke_angle: Twenty years of Mula Bandha at 5 a.m., and Boonchu is still 53, not 16. The only part of him acting like a teenager is his hamstrings: stiff, stubborn and not listening to the teacher.

kept.title: The peacock that digests the world's worst poison
kept.story: The Hatha Yoga Pradipika says Mayurasana, the peacock (hands on the floor, elbows at the navel, body straight like a stick), removes all diseases, digests too much bad food and destroys kalakuta. In legend, kalakuta is the poison that rose when the ocean was churned. Shiva held it in his throat to protect the world. No study has tested this.
kept.asana: Mayurasana (peacock), Ashtanga Intermediate Series, in the run Pincha Mayurasana, Karandavasana, Mayurasana, Nakrasana
kept.source: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 1.31 in modern editions (Muktibodhananda: 'Verse 31 Chapter 1'); Pancham Sinh 1914 labels it 1.33 (Sanskrit '...jarayet kala-kutam'). Sinh 1.32: 'Place the palms of both the hands on the ground, and place the navel on both the elbows and balancing thus, the body should be stretched backward like a stick.' Sinh 1.33: 'This Asana soon destroys all diseases... digests unwholesome food taken in excess, increases appetite and destroys the most deadly poison.' Muktibodhananda: 'enables destruction of kalakuta (a deadly poison).' Gheranda Samhita 2.29-30, tr. S. C. Vasu: 'it destroys the effects of deadly poisons'. Kalakuta: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Astika Parva, Section XVIII, tr. K. M. Ganguli (Project Gutenberg vol. 1): 'Siva, being solicited by Brahman, swallowed that poison for the safety of the creation. The divine Maheswara held it in his throat, and it is said that from that time he is called Nilakantha (blue-throated).'
kept.evidence: From the saved sacred-texts chapter 1 copy (live site 403): Sinh 1.32-1.33, Sanskrit 'jarayet kala-kutam', quotes exact. The item's 'balanced on both elbows' was slightly off: the text says palms on the ground with the navel on the elbows, so I fixed it. Muktibodhananda (archive.org) numbers the benefits verse 1.31 and names kalakuta. Gheranda 2.29-30 (Vasu scan) is exact and has the legs in Padmasana. I read Ganguli's Gutenberg text (ebook 15474): the passage is exact and ends 'So ends the eighteenth section in the Astika Parva of the Adi Parva.' I could not confirm that sacred-texts m01019.htm is Section XVIII (site blocked), so cite Gutenberg instead. The note that the BORI critical edition treats the episode as a mostly Southern-manuscript addition is reported only secondhand (an Advaita-l list citing Sukthankar's Prolegomena), so it is unverified. Intermediate Series placement is confirmed by ashtangayoga.info's Series 2 chart and NCSU's Ashtanga Intermediate chart.
kept.safety: Safe as written: Shiva is presented reverently as protector. I left out the gods-versus-asuras quarrel and the creatures killed in the churning (conflict and death rules). The poison and 'all diseases' claims are labelled as the text's legend and followed by 'No study has tested this'. Never suggest that an arm balance treats poisoning or illness: real poisoning needs emergency care. Mayurasana puts strong pressure on the belly, so it is not for pregnancy, hernia or a full stomach.
kept.joke_angle: Boonchu can hold Mayurasana, but his own digestion still loses to one plate of extra-spicy som tam from the market. Clearly he needs more peacock and fewer chillies.

kept.title: 8,400,000 asanas, one for every creature
kept.story: A legend in an old yoga text, the Gheranda Samhita, says Shiva described 8,400,000 asanas, as many as there are kinds of living creatures. Of these, 84 are the best, and 32 are useful for people. Maybe that is why so many asanas carry animal names: tortoise, rooster, frog, heron, crane, peacock, fish.
kept.asana: Animal asanas of Ashtanga: Kurmasana (tortoise) and Kukkutasana (rooster), Primary Series; Krounchasana (heron), Bhekasana (frog), Bakasana (crane), Mayurasana (peacock), Gomukhasana (cow face), Intermediate Series; Matsyasana (fish), Finishing Sequence.
kept.source: Gheranda Samhita 2.1-2.2, tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu, The Sacred Books of the Hindus vol. XV (Panini Office, Allahabad, 1914-15). Supporting: Hatha Yoga Pradipika, tr. Pancham Sinh (1914/1915), 1.35 in Sinh's numbering ('Siva taught 84 asanas'), 1.33 in common modern numbering.
kept.evidence: Opened the archive.org item (metadata: SBH vol. XV, Vasu, Siva Samhita + Gheranda Samhita) and its full OCR text. GS Lesson 2, v1: 'There are eighty-four hundreds of thousands [of Asanas described by Shiva]. The postures are as many in number as there are numbers of species of living creatures in this universe.' (that OCR drops the bracketed words; a second copy of the same Vasu translation, Sri Satguru 1979 reprint, has them). v2: 'Among them eighty-four are the best; and among these eighty-four, thirty-two have been found useful for mankind in this world.' The list of 32 in v3-6 itself is full of animals: cow-mouth, fish, peacock, cock, tortoise, frog, eagle, bull, locust, makara, camel, snake, lion. Sinh HYP (archive.org dli.csl.7087) v35: 'Siva taught 84 asanas.' Ashtanga links checked on AshtangaYoga.info series lists: Primary has Kurmasana and Kukkutasana; Intermediate PDF has Krounchasana, Bhekasana, Bakasana, Mayurasana and Gomukhasana; Finishing PDF has Matsyasana. Why I changed it: the text never says animal names come from the species count, so 'That is why' became 'Maybe that is why', and the story is now labelled as a legend.
kept.safety: Safe. A god is named only as the text names him, respectfully, and the story is labelled a legend. No violence, royalty, politics or health claims. On camera, keep the animal-name link as a 'maybe'.
kept.joke_angle: At one new asana a day, Boonchu will finish all 8,400,000 in about 23,000 years. With his hamstrings, call it 24,000. He has started with the rooster, since he is up at 4 a.m. anyway.

kept.title: 7,000, then 700, then 84
kept.story: In his 1934 book Yoga Makaranda, Krishnamacharya wrote that great teachers of the past knew tens of thousands of asanas. His teacher in Nepal, Ramamohana Brahmachari, had mastered 7,000, he wrote, and with his guidance Krishnamacharya mastered 700. The books of his day, he added, showed only 84.
kept.asana: The asana tradition Pattabhi Jois learned from Krishnamacharya, the root of the Ashtanga Primary and Intermediate Series
kept.source: T. Krishnamacharya, Yoga Makaranda (Kannada ed. 1934; Tamil ed. 1938), English tr. of the Tamil ed. by Lakshmi Ranganathan and Nandini Ranganathan (translators' note dated 15 Oct 2006), ch. 2.2 'Announcement', printed pp. 24-25 (PDF pp. 32-33). The citation said 'introduction, PDF p. 32'; the 7,000/700/84 lines are actually on printed p. 25 = PDF p. 33.
kept.evidence: Downloaded the terebess PDF (169 pages) and pulled out its text. Digits use a shifted font (Y=0, [=1, "=2, ]=3, a=4, b=5, c=6, d=7, e=8, f=9). This decoding checks out against the title page (Kannada ed. 1934, Tamil ed. 1938), the note date 'October 15, 2006' and the contents page numbers. PDF p. 33: 'In Nepal, living in Muktinarayanakshetram Sri Rama Mohana Brahmacari Guru Maharaj has mastered (brought into his experience) 7000 asanas. I have seen this directly and through his guidance and advice, I have mastered 700 asanas. Nowadays (in present times), there are only 84 asanas illustrated in the books available'. Earlier on the same page the figures are: Sankaracarya 84,000, Ramanujacarya 64,000, Madhvacarya and Vedanta Desikar 24,000, and Narasimha Bharati Swamigal 1,600 (which Krishnamacharya says he 'heard him state'). The Wikipedia article 'Tirumalai Krishnamacharya' cites YM p. 25 (Kannada ed. 1934) for the 7,000 and frames it as a 'tale'/claim, citing Singleton and Fraser 2014 on contradictory versions of his life. The same article lists K. Pattabhi Jois (1915-2009) as his pupil.
kept.safety: OK as rewritten, always as 'he wrote'. Leave out three things from the same passage and from the biography: (1) the kings and the Viceroy/palace patrons (royalty and politics); (2) the line about Vedas 'suppressed or hidden by people who abhor sanatana dharma' (religious conflict); (3) the claim of '84 lakh diseases' that asana and pranayama once cured (overstated health claim). Scholars doubt parts of this history, so never present it as fact.
kept.joke_angle: 7,000. Then 700. Then 84. After 20 years, Boonchu has fully mastered one: getting out of bed at 4 a.m. His hamstrings are still negotiating the other 83.

kept.title: Sweat, tremble, hop like a frog, walk on air
kept.story: An old yoga text, the Shiva Samhita, lists the stages of breath practice. First the body sweats. Then it trembles. Then the yogi jumps about "like a frog". Later, the text says, he walks in the air, and a yogi who can rise from the ground while sitting in Padmasana has mastered the air.
kept.asana: Utpluthih (lifting the body while seated in Padmasana), the last asana of the Ashtanga Finishing Sequence before Savasana. The link to the text is Boonchu's own: the verses describe pranayama, not this asana.
kept.source: Shiva Samhita 3.40-3.42 and 3.46, tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu (Panini Office, Allahabad, 1914; also in Sacred Books of the Hindus vol. XV, 1914-15). Supporting: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 2.12, tr. Pancham Sinh (1914).
kept.evidence: Opened the archive.org TheSivaSamhita text (Vasu, 'First published in 1914'). 3.41 matches word for word: 'In the second stage, there takes place the trembling of the body; in the third, the jumping about like a frog; and when the practice becomes greater, the adept walks in the air.' 3.42 matches: 'When the Yogi, though remaining in Padmasana, can rise in the air and leaves the ground, then know that he has gained Vayu-siddhi (success over air)'. The SBH XV scan has 'leave the ground'. 3.46 matches: 'he moves as the frog jumps over the ground, when frightened away by the clapping of hands.' 3.40 is the sweating stage. Sinh HYP (archive.org dli.csl.7087) 2.12 matches the shorter ladder: perspiration, quivering, steadiness. AshtangaYoga.info Finishing Sequence PDF order: ... Padmasana, Utpluthih, Savasana. Why I changed it: the title said 'fly', but the text says 'walks in the air'. The air-walking line also needed a 'the text says' label.
kept.safety: Levitation and walking on air are the text's claims, so label them and never imply viewers can or should achieve them. These are pranayama stages; do not give breath-retention instructions. Omit 3.44-3.46, which claim freedom from disease and that the yogi can eat anything or nothing (health claims). Omit 3.47 ('even were his life to come to the throat'). No violence, royalty or religious conflict.
kept.joke_angle: Bangkok gives Boonchu stage one for free: he sweats before he unrolls the mat. Twenty years of Utpluthih later, he has reached stage three, the frog, and he is staying there with great discipline.

kept.title: Rub the sweat in vs. sweat out the toxins
kept.story: Two old yoga texts say: rub your sweat into the skin, do not wipe it. The Hatha Yoga Pradipika says this makes the body strong. Detox ads say: sweat out toxins. A 2018 University of Ottawa calculation: two liters of sweat carry under a tenth of a nanogram of pollutants like PCBs. Your liver and kidneys do the cleaning.
kept.asana: Every Ashtanga practice; most visible in Surya Namaskara and the Primary Series in a hot Bangkok shala
kept.source: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 2.13, tr. Pancham Sinh (1914). Shiva Samhita 3.40, tr. S. C. Vasu (1914). Imbeault P, Ravanelli N, Chevrier J, 'Can POPs be substantially popped out through sweat?', Environment International 2018;111:131-132, doi:10.1016/j.envint.2017.11.023 (letter; University of Ottawa and McGill). Reported by Erika Engelhaupt, 'Can you really sweat out toxins?', National Geographic (first published 6 Apr 2018, updated 7 Aug 2023).
kept.evidence: Sinh HYP (archive.org dli.csl.7087) 2.13 matches word for word: 'The perspiration exuding from exertion of practice should be rubbed into the body (and not wiped), as by so doing the body becomes strong.' Vasu SS 3.40 matches: 'When it perspires, he should rub it well, otherwise the body of the Yogi loses its dhatu (humors).' The old story said 'vital essence', but Vasu has 'humors', so I fixed it. National Geographic quotes match: '45 minutes of high-intensity exercise could sweat a total of two liters in a day'; 'less than one-tenth of a nanogram of these pollutants'; '.02 percent of what you ingest every day'; 'more than 99 percent water'; 'That's what our kidneys and liver are for.' The pollutants are POPs ('pesticides, flame retardants, and PCBs'), and the figures are a calculation, not a lab trial. The PubMed record (via NCBI E-utilities) confirms the authors, journal, volume, pages and DOI, and lists it as a Letter/Comment. Bonus: Vasu's own introduction in SBH XV says 'Perspiration should be wiped off with a dry towel'. Housekeeping: this run accidentally overwrote scratchpad dl/hyp03.htm and dl/hyp04.htm with Cloudflare challenge pages. dl/hyp03.txt and dl/hyp04.txt are intact.
kept.safety: Present 'the body becomes strong' only as the old text's claim. No study shows that rubbing sweat in builds strength, so say so if asked. Say 'pollutants like PCBs' and 'calculation', not 'all toxins' or 'proved'. No gods, violence or politics. Do not suggest touching other people's sweat.
kept.joke_angle: Boonchu has rubbed his sweat back in every Bangkok morning for 20 years. By the old text, he should be the strongest 53-year-old in Thailand. His hamstrings did not read the old text.

kept.title: The Yoga Korunta: the lost book behind the practice
kept.story: As Pattabhi Jois told it, his teacher Krishnamacharya learned an old text, the Yoga Korunta, by heart from his own teacher. Its name is said to mean "groups": groups of asanas with vinyasa, drishti and bandhas. Krishnamacharya later studied a badly damaged copy in Calcutta. Jois never saw it, and no copy has been found.
kept.asana: The Ashtanga vinyasa method as a whole (Primary and Intermediate Series): asanas linked by vinyasa, with drishti and bandhas. It is not tied to one asana. Eddie Stern's foreword says the methods Jois was taught from 1927 were 'the methods from the Yoga Korunta'.
kept.source: Eddie Stern, Foreword (signed 'New York City, March 10, 2010') to Sri K. Pattabhi Jois, Yoga Mala (North Point Press / Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2010 edition; first English edition 1999). Glossary in the same book: 'Vamana is the author of Yoga Korunta, the authoritative text on asana and pranayama in ashtanga yoga.'
kept.evidence: I read a full-text copy of the 2010 edition. The foreword says, word for word: 'Guruji has often spoken about a text called the Yoga Korunta... Attributed to the sage Vamana, it was one of the many texts taught orally to Krishnamacharya, which he learned by heart during the seven and a half years he spent living with his teacher, Rama Mohan Brahmachari. Korunta means "groups," and the text was said to contain lists of many different groupings of asanas, as well as highly original teachings on vinyasa, drishti, bandhas, mudras, and philosophy. Before Krishnamacharya was sent off into the world to teach, around 1924, he was told that he could find this text in the Calcutta University Library. According to Guruji, who has never seen the text and doubted that it still exists, Krishnamacharya spent some time in Calcutta researching this book, which was badly damaged and had many missing portions.' The book's front matter has 'FOREWORD BY EDDIE STERN COPYRIGHT © 2010' and the foreword is signed 'March 10, 2010'. I also confirmed the glossary line about Vamana. All the facts in the draft match. What I fixed: (1) 'Korunta means groups' is Stern's explanation, not settled fact. Wikipedia (citing Hargreaves and Russell 2015) gives other suggestions, a Tamil form of 'yoga grantha' or a link to Kapalakurantaka, so the story now says 'is said to mean'. (2) The old title, 'a book nobody living has read', is a sceptical claim nobody can check, and it reads as a jab at the lineage. I replaced it. Wikipedia's article is sceptical (it is in the category 'Hoaxes in India'), so I did not follow it. The 'eaten by ants' detail is second-hand and stays out. Singleton's Yoga Body, pp. 184-186: I could not open the book, so do not quote it.
kept.safety: Safe as rewritten. There is no conflict, no kings and no harm in the story. The foreword's nearby paragraph mentions the maharaja of Mysore, so keep him out. Tell it neutrally, as a story Jois told, and give it respect: no 'myth-busting' tone, no hoax label, no tease about a missing book. Boonchu's authority comes from this lineage, so a sceptical framing would undercut his own positioning. It makes no health claims.
kept.joke_angle: Krishnamacharya learned whole books by heart. Boonchu, 53, learned the whole Primary Series by heart, and at 5 a.m. he still cannot remember where he put his reading glasses.

kept.title: The forward bend that slims the belly
kept.story: The Hatha Yoga Pradipika calls Paschimottanasana the foremost asana and says it "reduces obesity". There is no good evidence that one forward bend burns belly fat. In a 2007 study, 20 experienced practitioners did a 56-minute beginner yoga video: 2.5 METs on average, about 3.2 kcal a minute, like slow walking at 3.2 km/h.
kept.asana: Paschimottanasana, Ashtanga Primary Series. It is the first seated asana: number 11 in Yoga Mala (spelled 'Paschimattanasana'), right after Virabhadrasana.
kept.source: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 1.28-1.29 in modern numbering; Pancham Sinh translation (1914) numbers them 1.30-1.31: 'This Paschima Tana carries the air from the front to the back part of the body (i.e., to the susumna). It kindles gastric fire, reduces obesity and cures all diseases of men.' The Sanskrit has 'asanagryam' (foremost of asanas). Shiva Samhita 3.92-3.93, tr. Srisa Chandra Vasu (1914). Study: Hagins M, Moore W, Rundle A. 'Does practicing hatha yoga satisfy recommendations for intensity of physical activity which improves and maintains health and cardiovascular fitness?' BMC Complementary and Alternative Medicine 2007;7:40 (PMC2219995).
kept.evidence: HYP: I opened the Sinh 1914 text (sacred-texts mirror). Verse 31 matches the quote word for word, and the Sanskrit reads 'iti paschimatanam asanagryam', so 'foremost' is supported. Sinh's English leaves the word out. Yoga Mala also renders it 'Principle among asanas'. SHIVA SAMHITA: I opened Vasu 1914 (sourcelibrary.org scan). Verse 92 says: 'This is called Ugrasana (the stern-posture), it excites the motion of the air, destroys the dullness and uneasiness of the body, and is also called Paschimauttana'. Verse 93 says: 'Those who practice this obtain all the siddhis'. Both are correct, but I cut the siddhis line to keep the focus. HAGINS: I read the full text (Europe PMC). There were 20 intermediate-to-advanced practitioners, age 31.4 +/- 8.3, in a respiratory chamber. They did a 56-minute beginner-level hatha yoga video. The session means were HR 93.2 bpm, 49.4% of predicted max heart rate, 2.5 METs and 3.2 kcal/min, 'similar to walking on a treadmill at 3.2 kph', and significantly below the 3.0 MET moderate threshold. In the sun-salutation part, METs were 'not significantly different from' 3.0. Every number in the draft notes is correct. Caveat: the study session had no Paschimottanasana (its seated part was Lotus and Savasana), so it measures yoga sessions in general, not this asana. The story says only that, and does not claim the study tested the forward bend. I found no measured study of a full Ashtanga practice, so the story claims none. What I fixed: the old 'story' gave the text's claim, including 'cures all diseases', with no correction and no numbers.
kept.safety: Use with care. Yoga Mala itself, in Pattabhi Jois's benefits for Paschimattanasana, says it 'helps the stomach to become slender by dissolving its fat' and quotes this same HYP verse. Do not frame the Reel as 'Jois or the old texts were wrong'. Do not name Yoga Mala or mock the texts. Frame it as: the old texts speak of digestive fire and prana; modern measurements show yoga sessions are light activity; fitness comes from the whole practice and daily habits. Do not repeat 'cures all diseases' as a promise. Do not claim yoga 'does not burn calories' either. It is light activity, not zero. There is no violence, politics or royalty in it.
kept.joke_angle: Boonchu has folded forward every morning for 20 years. His hamstrings are still in negotiations, and his belly has not signed anything either.

kept.title: Does a twist wring out the liver?
kept.story: The Hatha Yoga Pradipika says Matsyendra's twist increases appetite, fights "the most deadly diseases" and wakes Kundalini. Today people say twists wring toxins out of the liver like a sponge. Dr Pam Peake of the American College of Sports Medicine calls this "squeeze and soak" idea "very inaccurate". Your liver and kidneys do that work all day.
kept.asana: Marichyasana C and D, Ashtanga Primary Series (numbers 18 and 19 in Yoga Mala). Pasasana and Ardha Matsyendrasana, Intermediate Series (Nadi Shodhana); AshtangaYoga.info lists both under the intermediate series. Note: the HYP describes the full Matsyendrasana, with the foot at the root of the thigh. Ashtanga practises the half version.
kept.source: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 1.26-1.27 in modern numbering (e.g. Muktibodhananda); Pancham Sinh translation (1914) numbers them 1.28-1.29: 'This is the asana, as explained by Sri Matsyanatha. It increases appetite and is an instrument for destroying the group of the most deadly diseases. Its practice awakens the Kundalini, stops the nectar shedding from the moon in people.' Correction: Amy Kraft, 'Reality check: Does yoga release toxins from the body?', CBS News, 15 April 2016, quoting Dr Pam Peake, Fellow and national spokesperson of the American College of Sports Medicine.
kept.evidence: HYP: I opened the Sinh 1914 text (sacred-texts mirror). Verses 28-29 match the quote word for word. The Sanskrit of verse 29 reads 'kundalini-prabodham chandra-sthiratvam cha dadati pumsam', so 'steadiness of the moon' is right. Warning: Sinh's English for how to do the asana (verse 28) is garbled into a bound, lotus-like grip. Quote only the effects line, never his instructions. The modern numbering (1.26-27) was confirmed only through search snippets for the Muktibodhananda edition. CBS: I opened the article. It is by Amy Kraft, 15 April 2016. Peake is quoted: 'The squeeze and soak theory is very inaccurate'. She also said 'Second by second, nanosecond by nanosecond, the human body is detoxing'. CBS reports that she said 1 percent of toxins at most leave through sweat. CORRECTION TO THE DRAFT NOTES: the line 'The liver and the kidneys also process toxins and excrete them as urine or stool' is NOT a Peake quote. It is CBS's own narration, unquoted. Attribute it to the article, not to her. No study measures toxins 'squeezed' from the liver by twisting. This correction rests on an expert statement and basic physiology, not trial numbers, so the Reel must not cite numbers for it.
kept.safety: Safe as rewritten. 'Destroying... deadly diseases' is quoted text about illness, not violence, and Matsyendra is named with respect. CBS says B.K.S. Iyengar popularised 'squeeze and soak'. Leave him out and do not make any teacher the target. Yoga Mala credits the Marichyasanas with digestive benefits, so frame this against the modern internet 'detox sponge' claim, not against Jois or the old texts. Leave out the sweat point (1 percent): it pulls in a second myth and brushes against Ashtanga's sweat culture. Do not promise any other health benefit in its place.
kept.joke_angle: The internet says twists wring out your liver like a sponge. After 20 years of 5 a.m. alarms and strong Thai coffee, Boonchu's liver does not want a squeeze. It wants a nap.

kept.title: Too old to build muscle
kept.story: The myth: after a certain age, you cannot build muscle. In a 1990 study, ten frail nursing-home residents, average age 90 and up to 96, did eight weeks of heavy leg weight training. In the nine who finished, strength rose 174% on average, thigh muscle grew 9%, and heel-to-toe walking speed improved 48%.
kept.asana: Utkatasana (vinyasa 1 of Surya Namaskara B; also in the Primary series right after Ardha Baddha Padmottanasana, before Virabhadrasana A). A thigh-strength relative of the training, not the same thing.
kept.source: Fiatarone MA, Marks EC, Ryan ND, Meredith CN, Lipsitz LA, Evans WJ. 'High-intensity strength training in nonagenarians. Effects on skeletal muscle.' JAMA 1990;263(22):3029-3034. PMID 2342214.
kept.evidence: The PubMed page is behind a cookie wall, so I pulled the same record (PMID 2342214) from Europe PMC. Abstract, verbatim: 'Ten frail, institutionalized volunteers aged 90 +/- 1 years undertook 8 weeks of high-intensity resistance training.' 'Strength gains averaged 174% +/- 31% (mean +/- SEM) in the 9 subjects who completed training. Midthigh muscle area increased 9.0% +/- 4.5%. Mean tandem gait speed improved 48% after training.' Conclusion: gains in 'muscle strength, size, and functional mobility among frail residents of nursing homes up to 96 years of age.' Every number in the draft matches. Asana check: the ashtangayoga.info Primary series list puts Utkatasana after Ardha Baddha Padmottanasana and before Virabhadrasana A. Its Surya Namaskara B breakdown has Utkatasana as vinyasa 1.
kept.safety: Clean: no war, violence, royalty, politics or religion. The participants are frail older people, so the joke must never be at their expense. Limits on the health claim: it was a tiny pilot (9 completers) with no control group, and the training was quadriceps work on weight machines, not yoga. Do not say Utkatasana gives 174%; say 'this is the muscle Utkatasana asks for'. 'Tandem gait' means heel-to-toe walking, not normal walking speed.
kept.joke_angle: Boonchu, flat: 'My excuse for skipping leg strength work was: I am 53. The oldest volunteer in this study was 96. My excuse lost by 43 years.'

kept.title: Too late to start in midlife
kept.story: The myth: if you did not exercise young, it is too late. A US study of 315,059 adults found that people inactive for most of adult life who became active at 40 to 61 had a 35% lower risk of dying during the study than the always-inactive. Lifelong very active people: 36% lower. Almost the same.
kept.asana: Surya Namaskara A (opens every Ashtanga practice and is the first sequence a beginner learns)
kept.source: Saint-Maurice PF, Coughlan D, Kelly SP, Keadle SK, Cook MB, Carlson SA, Fulton JE, Matthews CE. 'Association of Leisure-Time Physical Activity Across the Adult Life Course With All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality.' JAMA Network Open 2019;2(3):e190355. NIH-AARP Diet and Health Study. PMCID PMC6484624.
kept.evidence: The JAMA site returned 403, so I read the abstract and full text from Europe PMC (PMC6484624). 315,059 participants, '50 to 71 years of age at enrollment', mean follow-up 13.6 years. Late increasers (trajectory 2): 'those who increased LTPA only later in adulthood had 35% lower risk (trajectory 2: HR, 0.65; 95% CI, 0.62-0.68)'. The 0.64 figure is for people who 'maintained the highest amount of LTPA' (trajectory 10). Moderate lifelong maintainers (trajectory 7) had HR 0.71, and that is the group the authors call 'comparable'. Conclusion, verbatim: 'suggesting that midlife is not too late to start physical activity.' The draft numbers are right. I only made it clear that the 36% group is the most active lifelong group.
kept.safety: Mortality here is a statistic, not a death with victims, so it is fine. Keep the wording calm ('risk of dying during the study'). The study is observational, and activity was recalled at enrolment back to the teenage years (the authors list recall error as a limitation), so say 'linked to', never 'causes'. Do not imply Surya Namaskara A lowers death risk; the study measured any leisure-time activity, not yoga.
kept.joke_angle: Boonchu: 'Science says people who start exercising in their 40s end up almost level with lifelong exercisers. 35% versus 36%. I have set my alarm before sunrise for 20 years of Ashtanga. For one percent.'

kept.title: Older women shouldn't lift heavy
kept.story: The myth: women with weak bones should not lift heavy. In Australia's LIFTMOR trial, 101 women aged about 65 with low bone mass were split in two. Half lifted over 85% of their maximum, supervised, twice a week for 8 months. Their spine bone density rose 2.9%; the gentle home group lost 1.2%. Only one minor back spasm was reported.
kept.asana: Chaturanga Dandasana (in every Surya Namaskara and every vinyasa of every series). It is body weight only, so it is an analogy for strength work, not heavy lifting.
kept.source: Watson SL, Weeks BK, Weis LJ, Harding AT, Horan SA, Beck BR. 'High-Intensity Resistance and Impact Training Improves Bone Mineral Density and Physical Function in Postmenopausal Women With Osteopenia and Osteoporosis: The LIFTMOR Randomized Controlled Trial.' J Bone Miner Res 2018;33(2):211-220. Context: WHO 2020 guidelines (Bull FC et al., Br J Sports Med 2020;54(24):1451-1462) advise older adults to do 'varied multicomponent physical activity that emphasizes functional balance and strength training at moderate or greater intensity, on 3 or more days a week'.
kept.evidence: I read the abstract on Europe PMC and the OUP journal page. 'A total of 101 women (aged 65 +/- 5 years)'; 'HiRIT (n = 49) ... CON (n = 52)'; 'randomized to either 8 months of twice-weekly, 30-minute, supervised HiRIT (5 sets of 5 repetitions, >85% 1 repetition maximum) or a home-based, low-intensity exercise program'. Lumbar spine BMD '2.9 +/- 2.8% versus -1.2 +/- 2.8%'; femoral neck '0.3 versus -1.9%'. 'only one adverse event reported (HiRIT: minor lower back spasm)'. 'Contrary to current opinion, HiRIT was efficacious ... under highly supervised conditions'. Griffith University news pages confirm the trial ran on the Gold Coast and in Brisbane, Australia. FIX: the draft said all 101 women lifted heavy. Only 49 did; the other 52 were the gentle home group. I also renamed the title from 'Older people' to 'Older women', because the trial had only women in it.
kept.safety: Clean: no violence, royalty, politics or religion. Limits on the health claim: the women were screened, 'otherwise healthy' and closely supervised, and the program also included impact work (jumping chin-ups with drop landings). Never imply that anyone with osteoporosis should start heavy lifting alone; add 'with a qualified coach and your doctor's OK'. Chaturanga is body weight and was not studied, so do not claim it builds bone density.
kept.joke_angle: Boonchu, deadpan: 'Women of 65 in this trial lifted 85% of their maximum. I have done Chaturangas for 20 years. I still bend my knees to pick up my mat, because my hamstrings have never agreed to anything.'

kept.title: Unfit? It's just age
kept.story: The myth: losing fitness is just age. In 1966, five healthy 20-year-old men in Dallas volunteered to stay in bed for three weeks. Their aerobic fitness fell 27%. Thirty years later, ageing had cost them only about 11%. Bed did more harm than birthdays. Six months of endurance training at about 50 brought them back to their 1966 starting level.
kept.asana: Savasana (the final rest after Utpluthih at the end of the finishing sequence of every series)
kept.source: Mitchell JH, Levine BD, McGuire DK. 'The Dallas Bed Rest and Training Study: Revisited After 50 Years.' Circulation 2019;140(16):1293-1295. McGuire DK et al. 'A 30-year follow-up of the Dallas Bedrest and Training Study: I. Effect of age on the cardiovascular response to exercise.' Circulation 2001;104(12):1350-1357 (PMID 11560849). Part II: 'Effect of age on cardiovascular adaptation to exercise training.' Circulation 2001;104(12):1358-1366 (PMID 11560850).
kept.evidence: PMC6814251 (2019): five men, age 20 in 1966, 3 weeks of 'complete bed rest'; 'Average VO2max declined 27% after bed rest'; 'baseline VO2max had declined by 12% over the 30-year interval'; '3 weeks of bed rest at age 20 reduced cardiovascular capacity more than 30 years of aging.' Europe PMC abstracts: Part I says 'VO(2)max decreased 11% (3.30 versus 2.90 L/min)', body fat went from '14% versus 28%', and '3 weeks of bedrest ... had a more profound impact on physical work capacity than did 3 decades of aging.' Part II: a 6-month program raised VO2max 14%, 'achieving the level observed at the baseline evaluations 30 years before'; but 'no subject achieved the same maximal VO(2) attained after training 30 years earlier.' Savasana: the ashtangayoga.info finishing cheat sheet lists Baddha Padmasana, Yoga Mudra, Padmasana, Utplutih, Savasana, 'relax 10-20 minutes'. FIX: the draft title said 'Stiff', but the study measured only aerobic fitness, never stiffness or flexibility.
kept.safety: Clean: no violence, royalty, politics or religion. There were only 5 men. Say 'aerobic fitness', not 'flexibility' or 'stiffness'. Do not suggest that rest or Savasana is harmful; the point is weeks of inactivity, not minutes of rest. Caveat for the curious: a 40-year follow-up (McGavock et al., J Gerontol A 2009;64(2):293-299) found that by about age 60 the 40-year decline (26%) had caught up with the bed-rest drop (27%). So do not stretch the 'bed beats birthdays' line beyond age 50.
kept.joke_angle: Boonchu: 'Three weeks in bed did more harm than 30 years of birthdays. Now when my alarm rings before sunrise, I call it anti-ageing science. My body still votes for the bed.'

kept.title: 10,000 steps is a medical rule
kept.story: The 10,000 steps goal likely came from a 1965 Japanese pedometer named Manpo-kei, '10,000-step meter'. In a Harvard study of 16,741 women averaging 72, about 4,400 steps a day was linked to a 41% lower death rate than 2,700, with benefits levelling off near 7,500. For adults under 60, a 2022 review put the level-off at 8,000 to 10,000.
kept.asana: Samasthitih (the standing position that opens and closes every Surya Namaskara and each vinyasa count; Ashtanga counts breaths, not steps)
kept.source: Lee IM, Shiroma EJ, Kamada M, Bassett DR, Matthews CE, Buring JE. 'Association of Step Volume and Intensity With All-Cause Mortality in Older Women.' JAMA Intern Med 2019;179(8):1105-1112, doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2019.0899. Paluch AE et al. 'Daily steps and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of 15 international cohorts.' Lancet Public Health 2022;7(3):e219-e228 (PMC9289978). Asana: ashtangayoga.info Surya Namaskara A sequence page (ends in Samasthitih).
kept.evidence: Opened PMC6547157 (full text). Confirmed: the 10,000 goal 'likely derives from the trade name of a pedometer sold in 1965 by Yamasa Clock and Instrument Company in Japan' (Manpo-kei); 16,741 women, mean age 72; quartile medians 2,718 / 4,363 / 5,905 / 8,442 steps; adjusted HR 0.59 for quartile 2; Discussion states about 4,400 steps/d was 'associated with a 41% reduction in mortality rate'; risk declined 'until approximately 7500 steps/d, after which they leveled'. Opened PMC9289978 (Paluch 2022): 47,471 adults, 15 studies; risk decreased 'until 6000-8000 steps per day' for 60+ and 'until 8000-10 000 steps per day' for under 60. FIX reason: original story was accurate but implied 10,000 is pointless; Paluch shows 8,000 to 10,000 is still the plateau for under-60s, so the under-60 line was added for fairness. Samasthitih confirmed as start/end of Surya Namaskara A on ashtangayoga.info.
kept.safety: Safe. Japan as a friendly product-label origin, no conflict. 'Death rate' is a study statistic, not a story with victims. Observational data: keep the word 'linked', never 'causes' or 'adds years'. Leave out the folk claim that the character 10,000 looks like a walking man (not in Lee's paper).
kept.joke_angle: 'I'm 53. The science says under 60, my number is still 8,000 to 10,000 steps. So a 1965 shop label still has me on its list. I take about 40 steps from bed to mat at 4 a.m. The rest I call vinyasa.' True line after: past 60, 6,000 to 8,000 does most of the work.

kept.title: Muscle turns into fat
kept.story: The myth: stop training and muscle 'turns into fat'. In a 2007 study, 18 young adults kept one leg off the ground for four weeks. Thigh muscle shrank 7.4% and calf 7.9%, while fat between the muscles grew 14.5% and 20%. Two different tissues moved in opposite directions. Muscle did not become fat.
kept.asana: Utthita Hasta Padangusthasana A and B (standing one-leg balance that opens the Primary series after the fundamental standing sequence)
kept.source: Manini TM, Clark BC, Nalls MA, Goodpaster BH, Ploutz-Snyder LL, Harris TB. 'Reduced physical activity increases intermuscular adipose tissue in healthy young adults.' Am J Clin Nutr 2007;85(2):377-384, doi:10.1093/ajcn/85.2.377. Asana: ashtangayoga.info Primary Series (Yoga Cikitsa) list.
kept.evidence: Pulled the abstract from Europe PMC (DOI 10.1093/ajcn/85.2.377): '6 men and 12 women aged 19-28 y underwent a 4-wk control period, which was followed by 4 wk of unilateral lower limb suspension'; 'decreased thigh and calf muscle volumes by 7.4% and 7.9%'; 'no significant change in subcutaneous adipose tissue'; IMAT increase 'larger in the calf (20%) than in the thigh (14.5%)'; strength loss thigh 20.4%, calf 15%. All numbers in the story match. Opened ashtangayoga.info Primary Series page: Utthita Hasta Padangusthasana A is listed #1 and B #3 of the Primary series proper.
kept.safety: Safe. No health overclaim: the story only says the tissues are different and moved in opposite directions. Small study (18 people), short time, healthy young adults. Do not say exercise 'prevents' fat gain from this study alone.
kept.joke_angle: 'I asked my left hamstring why it is so stiff. It said it has been on holiday since 2006, because the right leg does all the work in Utthita Hasta Padangusthasana. Twenty years of practice and my two legs still are not on speaking terms.'

kept.title: Sweat means fat is melting
kept.story: Sweat is mostly water and salt, not fat. Burned fat mostly leaves through the lungs: of 10 kg lost, 8.4 kg is breathed out as carbon dioxide and 1.6 kg becomes water. Two Sydney researchers asked 150 doctors, dietitians and personal trainers where lost fat goes. Only three got it right. Breathing faster does not burn more fat.
kept.asana: No single asana: the deep, even breathing with sound through every vinyasa (all series). Do not label it 'ujjayi': Sharath Jois taught 'normal breath, inhalation and exhalation with sound' and said 'Ujjayi breath is a type of pranayama' (KPJAYI conference, March 2013).
kept.source: Meerman R, Brown AJ. 'When somebody loses weight, where does the fat go?' BMJ 2014;349:g7257 (Christmas issue), doi:10.1136/bmj.g7257. UNSW Newsroom, 14 March 2018, by Ruben Meerman and Andrew Brown. Breath wording: Conference notes with Sharath Jois, KPJAYI, March 2013 (archive.joisyoga.com).
kept.evidence: Opened the UNSW Newsroom article (Meerman and Brown, 14 March 2018): 'If you lose 10kg of fat, precisely 8.4kg comes out through your lungs and the remaining 1.6kg turns into water'; of 'the 150 doctors, dietitians and personal trainers we surveyed', only three gave the correct answer. BMJ 2014 figures (29 kg oxygen in, 28 kg CO2 and 11 kg water out for 10 kg fat) confirmed via NPR and ScienceDaily coverage of the paper. Opened archive.joisyoga.com 2013 conference notes: Sharath says 'You do normal breath, inhalation and exhalation with sound. Ujjayi breath is a type of pranayama.' FIX reason: the facts are right, but the asana line used the 'ujjayi' label, which contradicts Sharath's own teaching. For a teacher authorized by Sharath this would be a lineage error on camera. Also added the line that faster breathing does not burn more fat, and 'mostly water and salt' for accuracy.
kept.safety: Safe. Keep the line that breathing faster does not burn more fat; the CO2 comes from metabolism, and over-breathing only makes people dizzy. Do not present Ashtanga breathing as a fat-loss method. Avoid the 'ujjayi' label to stay true to Sharath's teaching.
kept.joke_angle: 'In Bangkok I lose ___ kilos of sweat every Mysore class. It all comes back with one coconut. The fat leaves the slow way, out through my mouth, one breath at a time. After 20 years of practice, I can confirm it is very slow.'

kept.title: No pain, no gain
kept.story: The myth: if you are not sore, it did not work. In a 2016 study, ten young men trained their legs for ten weeks. Muscle damage was highest in week one, but it did not predict growth. Growth matched the muscle building at weeks 3 and 10, as damage faded. Soreness is a poor scorecard.
kept.asana: Navasana (five rounds with a lift-up between rounds, seated section of the Primary series)
kept.source: Damas F, Phillips SM, Libardi CA, Vechin FC, Lixandrao ME, Jannig PR, Costa LA, Bacurau AV, Snijders T, Parise G, Tricoli V, Roschel H, Ugrinowitsch C. 'Resistance training-induced changes in integrated myofibrillar protein synthesis are related to hypertrophy only after attenuation of muscle damage.' J Physiol 2016;594(18):5209-5222, doi:10.1113/JP272472, PMID 27219125, PMC5023708. Asana: ashtangayoga.info Primary Series list (Navasana #23); KinoYoga (Kino MacGregor) on five rounds.
kept.evidence: Opened PMC5023708 (full text). 'Ten young men (27 (1) years, mean (SEM))'; 10 weeks, twice a week, 19 sessions of leg press and leg extension. 'Muscle damage (Z-band streaming) was the highest during post-RE recovery at T1, lower at T2 and minimal at T3.' 'When muscle damage was the highest, so was the integrated MyoPS (at T1), but neither were related to hypertrophy; however, integrated MyoPS at T2 and T3 were correlated with hypertrophy.' Table 2 r values 0.864 to 0.946 (abstract rounds to about 0.9). T1 is the first week; soreness was also highest then. Navasana: ashtangayoga.info lists it in the Primary series; kinoyoga.com says it is held 'for five breaths, five times in a row with a lift-up for a break between repetitions'. (ashtangayoga.info's own Navasana page says three to five times, so 'five rounds' is the Mysore norm.)
kept.safety: Safe. Small study (10 men, average age 27) about muscle growth only, not general health or injury. Add a spoken true line after the joke: sharp pain or joint pain is a stop sign, not a sign of progress. Do not say soreness is harmful, only that it is a poor measure of growth.
kept.joke_angle: 'I have been sore after Navasana for 20 years. By the no-pain-no-gain rule, I should look like a bodybuilder by now. Instead I look like a 53-year-old man whose legs still will not go straight in the boat.'

kept.title: Only hard, sweaty exercise counts
kept.story: The myth: gentle movement does not count. A 2019 BMJ study combined data from 36,383 adults, average age 63, who wore activity trackers. People in the top quarter for light movement had 62% lower risk of early death than the bottom quarter. The biggest gain came from the first step up: about one extra hour a day.
kept.asana: Surya Namaskara A, the first movement of every series (ashtangayoga.info: five rounds at the start of practice). Use it only as a picture of 'the first step'; it is not light-intensity activity. The draft link, the finishing sequence, was replaced: it includes shoulderstand and headstand, so it is the wrong thing to point at for older viewers who cannot do a full practice.
kept.source: Ekelund U, Tarp J, Steene-Johannessen J, Hansen BH, Jefferis B, et al., Lee IM. 'Dose-response associations between accelerometry measured physical activity and sedentary time and all cause mortality: systematic review and harmonised meta-analysis.' BMJ 2019;366:l4570 (PMID 31434697, PMC6699591). Light activity HRs by quarter (model B): 1.00, 0.60, 0.44, 0.38. Sedentary time: 1.00, 1.28, 1.71, 2.63. WHO physical activity fact sheet: 'any amount of physical activity is better than none'.
kept.evidence: BMJ site gave 403, so I read the Europe PMC abstract and the PMC full text. Confirmed: 8 cohorts, n=36,383, mean age 62.6, 72.8% women, median follow-up 5.8 years; light activity HRs 1.00/0.60/0.44/0.38; sedentary HR 2.63. The full text says the biggest risk drop was second quarter vs referent, and the gap between those two light-activity quarters was about 60 min/day. Model B adjusts for age, sex, BMI, socioeconomic position and wear time, but NOT for moderate-to-vigorous activity, so the draft's 'light-intensity movement alone' overstates it and was removed. All studies were in the US and western Europe, ages 40+, observational; the authors say reverse causation might persist. WHO fact sheet quote checked word for word. Note: the WHO fact sheet does not contain a 'more is better' line.
kept.safety: Passes after the fix. No violence, politics, royalty or religion. Mortality is given as a statistic, not a story with victims. Keep the wording 'lower risk' and 'linked to', not 'adds years'. Do not use the finishing sequence as the suggestion for frail or older viewers because of the inversions. Only use the stairs/cake skeleton if it really happened.
kept.joke_angle: 'A study says the first hour of gentle movement does the most good. I get up at 4 a.m. for Ashtanga. By the time students arrive, I have already done my most important exercise of the day: looking for my glasses.'

kept.title: Stretch first and you won't get injured
kept.story: The myth: a quick stretch before exercise prevents injury. A 2014 review of 25 trials and 26,610 people found stretching made no real difference to sports injuries, while strength training cut them to under a third. A Cochrane review found stretching lowered next-day soreness by only half a point to one point on a 100-point scale.
kept.asana: Padangusthasana and Padahastasana: confirmed as the first two of the standing fundamentals, which come straight after the sun salutations (ashtangayoga.info fundamentals list and series overview).
kept.source: Lauersen JB, Bertelsen DM, Andersen LB. Br J Sports Med 2014;48(11):871-877 (PMID 24100287): stretching RR 0.963 (0.846-1.095); strength training RR 0.315 (0.207-0.480); proprioception RR 0.550; multiple exposures RR 0.655. Herbert RD, de Noronha M, Kamper SJ. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2011;(7):CD004577 (PMID 21735398): 12 studies; pre-exercise stretching -0.52 and post-exercise -1.04 on a 100-point scale at one day.
kept.evidence: Read both abstracts on Europe PMC (the PubMed page needed cookies). Lauersen: 25 trials, 26,610 participants, 3,464 injuries; the RRs match the draft exactly; the authors write 'Strength training reduced sports injuries to less than 1/3'. Cochrane: half a point before exercise, about one point after. The draft's single 'about one point' applied only to after-exercise stretching, so it was corrected to 'half a point to one point'. Cochrane covered any stretching technique, not only static stretching. The strength result comes from only a few trials with wide CIs, so 'under a third' should stay tied to these trials. Ashtanga order confirmed on ashtangayoga.info.
kept.safety: Passes. The story does not mention the military-recruit trials that Lauersen pooled, as the notes require. No overstated claim: it does not say Ashtanga's order prevents injury. It only says moving first is how the practice is built. Stretching still improves range of motion, so do not say 'stretching is useless'.
kept.joke_angle: (Flat) 'Stretch first so you won't get hurt.' (Second voice) 'I have stretched my hamstrings every morning for twenty years. They still have not heard about it.'

kept.title: Flexibility is gone for good after 60
kept.story: The myth: after 60, stiffness is permanent. A 2019 review of 22 randomised trials in adults with an average age of 60 or more found that yoga, compared with no exercise, improved lower-body flexibility, balance and leg strength. The gains were moderate, not miracles, but the body still answered practice.
kept.asana: Paschimottanasana: confirmed in the seated part of the Primary series (A to D, ashtangayoga.info Primary series list).
kept.source: Sivaramakrishnan D, Fitzsimons C, Kelly P, Ludwig K, Mutrie N, Saunders DH, Baker G. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act 2019;16:33 (PMID 30953508, PMC6451238). Compared with inactive controls, Hedges' g: balance 0.7, lower-body flexibility 0.5, lower-limb strength 0.45. Supporting: Araujo CGS, ..., Fiatarone Singh MA, et al. Scand J Med Sci Sports 2024;34(8):e14708 (PMID 39165228).
kept.evidence: The journal page redirected to a login, so I read the Europe PMC abstract. Confirmed: 27 records from 22 RCTs, inclusion was mean age 60+ with no specific disease, and the effect sizes match. Only 17 of the 22 RCTs measured physical function. 'Inactive controls' means wait-list or education booklets, so 'no exercise' is fair. Araujo 2024 abstract confirmed: 3,139 adults aged 46-65, mean follow-up 12.9 years, HR 1.87 for men and 4.78 for women, Flexindex 35% higher in women. The women's CI is very wide (1.23 to 31.71), so do not lean on 4.78. The callback is checked: Fiatarone MA et al., JAMA 1990, 10 frail volunteers aged about 90, 8 weeks of strength training. Araujo's co-author is listed as Fiatarone Singh MA.
kept.safety: Passes. The trials studied yoga in general, not Ashtanga, so do not say 'Ashtanga reverses ageing'. The effect sizes are moderate. If the Araujo mortality numbers are used, frame them as 'linked to', since the study is observational. The 'women are 35% more flexible' joke must target Boonchu only, never female students.
kept.joke_angle: 'Research says flexibility still improves after 60. Good news for me: I am 53, so my hamstrings have seven more years before they have to start listening.'

kept.title: Getting up off the floor means nothing
kept.story: The myth: getting up off the floor means nothing. Brazilian researchers scored 2,002 adults aged 51 to 80 on sitting down and standing up with no help from hands or knees (0 to 10). Over about six years, each extra point was linked to 21% better survival; the lowest scorers had over five times the risk of the top scorers.
kept.asana: Seated vinyasa (jump back and jump through between seated asanas, Primary series) and Utpluthih (14th of 15 in the finishing sequence, lifting the lotus seat on the arms; ashtangayoga.info finishing list). These are thematic links only. The test itself is plain sit-down, stand-up.
kept.source: Brito LB, Ricardo DR, Araujo DS, Ramos PS, Myers J, Araujo CG. 'Ability to sit and rise from the floor as a predictor of all-cause mortality.' Eur J Prev Cardiol 2014;21(7):892-898 (PMID 23242910; online 2012). Median follow-up 6.3 years; HRs adjusted for age, sex and BMI: 5.44 (scores 0-3), 3.44, 1.84 vs 8-10; each point linked to 21% better survival.
kept.evidence: Read the Europe PMC abstract. Confirmed: 2,002 adults aged 51-80 (68% men); 0-5 each for sitting and rising, minus one point per hand or knee support, 0-10 total; median follow-up 6.3 years; 159 deaths (7.9%); HR 5.44 for 0-3 vs 8-10; 'each unit increase in SRT score conferred a 21% improvement in survival'. It is a retrospective cohort from one clinic, so the result is observational. I changed 'Brazilian doctors' to 'researchers' because not every author is confirmed as a physician.
kept.safety: Passes. Say 'linked to living longer', not 'predicts death'. The risk is a statistic with no victims named. For a Reel demo, show older or frail viewers trying it next to a chair or with someone beside them. Do not suggest jump-throughs or Utpluthih to beginners as a fix.
kept.joke_angle: 'I took the sit-and-rise test at 53. No hands, no knees. I took half a point off for the noise my knees made. The study does not score that. I scored it anyway.' (Pairs with skeleton #4: 'the hardest asana is getting up off the floor without a sound.')

kept.title: You have to be flexible before you start
kept.story: Myth: you must be flexible to start. Patanjali's Yoga Sutra 2.46 defines asana as 'stable-and-easy posture' (Woods translation, 1914). Toes are not mentioned. In a trial published in 2016, 118 inactive adults, average age 62, did hatha yoga three times a week for 8 weeks. Their flexibility improved, about as much as a stretching-and-strength group.
kept.asana: Paschimottanasana A-D (Primary Series seated sequence); Uttanasana, the forward fold inside Surya Namaskara A and B, which open every Ashtanga series
kept.source: Patanjali, Yoga Sutra 2.46, tr. James Haughton Woods, The Yoga-System of Patanjali, Harvard Oriental Series vol. 17 (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 1914): '46. Stable-and-easy posture.' Gothe NP, McAuley E. 'Yoga Is as Good as Stretching-Strengthening Exercises in Improving Functional Fitness Outcomes: Results From a Randomized Controlled Trial.' J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci 2016;71(3):406-411 (online Aug 2015). doi:10.1093/gerona/glv127. Woods scan: https://archive.org/details/yogasystemofpata00wooduoft
kept.evidence: Opened the Gothe & McAuley full text at PMC5864160. It confirms N=118 randomized (yoga 61, stretching-strengthening 57; 108 finished), mean age 62.0 (range 55-79), sedentary for at least 6 months, 8 weeks, 3 x 1 hour hatha yoga per week. Both groups improved significantly on sit-and-reach and back-scratch. The authors conclude yoga was 'just as effective', not better; the only group difference was left-leg balance, which favoured yoga. sacred-texts.com returned HTTP 403 to every request, so I could not confirm BonGiovanni's wording 'The posture should be steady and comfortable'. I replaced it with the Woods 1914 Harvard translation, which I read in a saved full-text copy: '46. Stable-and-easy posture.' Woods's commentary then lists seated examples (lotus, hero, staff and others) and never mentions toes. I also changed 'the whole definition' to 'defines', because sutras 2.47-2.48 go on to discuss asana. Asana check: the Primary Series practice sheet (ashtangayoga.info, Dr. Ronald Steiner, 2015) lists Paschimottanasana A B C D. Bonus line confirmed in the Penman et al. 2012 full text (Int J Yoga 5(2):92-101, PMC3410203; 2,567 practitioners): 'increased flexibility/muscle tone' was among the top reasons for starting yoga (about 71%), and the paper says respondents 'commonly started practicing yoga for muscle tone and flexibility'.
kept.safety: Safe: no violence, royalty, politics or mocking of Patanjali or the lineage. Health claims are kept modest: the story says 'improved' and 'about as much as', never 'beat' or 'cures stiffness'. The trial participants were 55-79 and inactive, so do not imply the same result for every age or for injured people. If you want 'steady and comfortable' on screen, call it a common paraphrase of sthira-sukham-asanam, not a quote from a named translator, unless you can open the BonGiovanni page yourself.
kept.joke_angle: Twenty years of Paschimottanasana, and Boonchu's toes are still 'a long-term project'. Good news: Patanjali's definition never mentions toes. Boonchu checked. Twice. At 5 a.m., while still unable to reach them.

kept.title: Yoga is just stretching
kept.story: Myth: yoga is only stretching. In a small 2001 study, 10 untrained young adults did hatha yoga at least twice a week for 8 weeks. Elbow strength rose 31% and knee-muscle endurance 57%. In 2011, six trained young people doing four rounds of Sun Salutation averaged 80% of their predicted maximum heart rate, reaching 90% in round four.
kept.asana: Chaturanga Dandasana inside Surya Namaskara A and B, which open every Ashtanga series
kept.source: Tran MD, Holly RG, Lashbrook J, Amsterdam EA. 'Effects of Hatha Yoga Practice on the Health-Related Aspects of Physical Fitness.' Preventive Cardiology 2001;4(4):165-170. doi:10.1111/j.1520-037x.2001.00542.x (PMID 11832673). Mody BS. 'Acute effects of Surya Namaskar on the cardiovascular & metabolic system.' J Bodyw Mov Ther 2011;15(3):343-347. doi:10.1016/j.jbmt.2010.05.001 (PMID 21665111). Counterweight: Hagins M, Moore W, Rundle A. BMC Complement Altern Med 2007;7:40. doi:10.1186/1472-6882-7-40 (PMID 18053143).
kept.evidence: The PubMed pages served only a cookie notice, so I pulled the official abstracts through NCBI E-utilities. Tran 2001 abstract: 10 healthy untrained volunteers (9 women, 1 man), ages 18-27, a minimum of two classes a week for 8 weeks, no control group. Isokinetic strength rose 31% (elbow extension), 19% (elbow flexion) and 28% (knee extension). Isometric knee-flexion endurance rose 57%. VO2max rose 7% (absolute) and 6% (relative). Mody 2011 abstract: 6 Asian Indian men and women aged 18-22, trained in Surya Namaskar for over 2 years, one session of four rounds. Heart rate was 80% of age-predicted HRmax in round 2, 84% in round 3 and 90% in round 4, averaging 80%. About 230 kcal per 30 minutes for a 60 kg person. Hagins 2007 abstract: a 56-minute beginner hatha video averaged 49.4% of predicted max heart rate, similar to walking at 3.2 km/h. The authors add that sun salutation bouts over 10 minutes may give enough intensity for unfit people. My story edits: 'at least twice a week' and 'predicted maximum heart rate' match the abstracts exactly. 'Trained' is added because Mody's subjects had 2+ years of practice. Asana check: Surya Namaskara A and B open the practice on the ashtangayoga.info sheets (Steiner 2015), and Chaturanga Dandasana is a standard step in both.
kept.safety: Safe: no violence, royalty, politics or mockery. Both studies are tiny (10 and 6 people), and Tran had no control group, so present them as 'small studies show', not proof. Mody's Surya Namaskar is a classic 12-step version, not identical to Ashtanga's A and B. Do not claim weight loss or 'better than the gym'. Pair it with the Hagins counterweight if a caption needs honesty about gentle classes.
kept.joke_angle: Boonchu tells new students it is 'gentle stretching'. By the fifth Surya Namaskara, his own shirt has filed a complaint and is asking for a transfer to a less sweaty teacher.

kept.title: After 60, balance is just gone
kept.story: Myth: after 60, balance is simply gone. A 2016 review pooled six trials with 307 people aged 60 and over. Yoga gave a small improvement in balance and a medium improvement in mobility, meaning getting up and moving around. The authors say we do not yet know if this prevents falls.
kept.asana: Utthita Hasta Padangusthasana and Ardha Baddha Padmottanasana (standing sequence, Primary Series)
kept.source: Youkhana S, Dean CM, Wolff M, Sherrington C, Tiedemann A. 'Yoga-based exercise improves balance and mobility in people aged 60 and over: a systematic review and meta-analysis.' Age and Ageing 2016;45(1):21-29 (online 25 Dec 2015). doi:10.1093/ageing/afv175 (PMID 26707903).
kept.evidence: I pulled the abstract through NCBI E-utilities because PubMed served only a cookie notice. It confirms 6 trials and 307 participants aged 60+. Balance: Hedges' g = 0.40 (95% CI 0.15-0.65; 6 trials), described as a small effect. Physical mobility: g = 0.50 (95% CI 0.06-0.95; 3 trials), described as a medium effect. The conclusion says further research is needed to know whether these gains prevent falls. The objective section says one-third of community-dwelling older adults fall each year and that exercise which challenges balance is proven to prevent falls. Asana check: the Primary Series sheet (ashtangayoga.info, Steiner 2015) lists both Utthita Hasta Padangusthasana and (Utthita Parsvasahita) Ardha Baddha Padmottanasana in the standing part of the series. The story keeps the authors' 'small' and 'medium' wording and drops the effect-size numbers to keep it plain.
kept.safety: Safe: falls are mentioned only as an open question, with no injuries or victims described. Never say 'yoga prevents falls'. The authors say that is unproven. Note that the mobility result rests on only 3 trials with a wide confidence interval. Older viewers with balance problems should be told to practise near a wall or under supervision. Do not present this as medical advice.
kept.joke_angle: Boonchu is 53, so he has seven years before this study is officially about him. Judging by his wobble in Utthita Hasta Padangusthasana this morning, he has started training for it early.

kept.title: Ashtanga is only for the young
kept.story: Myth: Ashtanga is for twenty-year-olds.
