The Hatha Yoga Pradipika, a 15th-century yoga text, says: 'Whether young, old or too old, sick or lean, one who discards laziness, gets success if he practises Yoga' (chapter 1, verse 66, Pancham Sinh, 1914). Age is not the test. The only person the verse leaves out is the lazy one.
kept.asana: The whole practice; Surya Namaskara A and B as the daily start of every Ashtanga series
kept.source: Svatmarama, Hatha Yoga Pradipika, chapter 1 ('On Asanas'), English verse 66 in Pancham Sinh's translation (Allahabad: Panini Office, 1914; printed as Sacred Books of the Hindus vol. XV part III, dated January 1915). On the sacred-texts page, the Sanskrit line 'yuvo vrddho 'tivrddho va vyadhito durbalo 'pi va...' carries the number 67. Other editions number it differently.
kept.evidence: sacred-texts.com returned 403 to live requests. I read a saved copy of the same page ('Hatha Yoga Pradipika, tr. by Pancham Sinh, [1914], at sacred-texts.com', Chapter 1, On Asanas), which says word for word: 'Whether young, old or too old, sick or lean, one who discards laziness, gets success if he practises Yoga. 66.' The next verse says success comes only from practice, not from reading books. I cross-checked against a scanned Sinh print (Sacred Books of the Hindus vol. XV part III, Jan 1915), which has the same wording and English verse number 66. I could not confirm the claim that 'other editions' number it 1.64, so the story cites Sinh's numbering only. No primary source was found for the 'anyone can practise except lazy people' line attributed to Pattabhi Jois, so it stays out. Dating the text to the 15th century is the standard scholarly dating for Svatmarama.
kept.safety: Safe: a verbatim quote with no violence, royalty or religious conflict, and nothing that mocks Svatmarama, Jois or the lineage. The lazy-person line targets laziness in general, not any group. In this verse, 'success' means progress in yoga, not a cure, so do not present 'sick... gets success' as a health or healing promise. If space is tight, cut 'sick or lean' with an ellipsis rather than paraphrasing it as a medical claim. Do not put the unsourced Jois 'lazy people' quote on screen.
kept.joke_angle: The verse lists young, old and too old. Boonchu, 53, is still deciding which line to stand in. His 4:30 a.m. alarm and his hamstrings have already voted, and the result was not 'young'.

kept.title: No upside-down after 50
kept.story: Myth: after 50, going upside down turns dangerous. In a 2006 study of 75 yoga practitioners, headstand doubled eye pressure, and age did not predict the rise. In a small 2015 study, Downward Dog raised it most of four head-down asanas (17 to 29 mmHg), back to normal two minutes after sitting up. Glaucoma? Ask your eye doctor first.
kept.asana: Sirsasana (finishing sequence; tested in the 2006 study); Halasana (finishing sequence; tested in 2015); Adho Mukha Svanasana and the Uttanasana forward fold (inside Surya Namaskara A and B; tested in 2015). The 2015 'Viparita Karani' was legs up the wall, which is not in the Ashtanga series.
kept.source: Baskaran M, Raman K, Ramani KK, Roy J, Vijaya L, Badrinath SS. 'Intraocular pressure changes and ocular biometry during Sirsasana (headstand posture) in yoga practitioners.' Ophthalmology 2006;113(8):1327-1332. doi:10.1016/j.ophtha.2006.02.063 (PMID 16806478). Jasien JV, Jonas JB, de Moraes CG, Ritch R. 'Intraocular Pressure Rise in Subjects with and without Glaucoma during Four Common Yoga Positions.' PLoS ONE 2015;10(12):e0144505. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0144505. NCCIH, 'Yoga: What You Need To Know' (last updated August 2023). Cramer H, Krucoff C, Dobos G. PLoS ONE 2013;8(10):e75515.
kept.evidence: Opened the PLoS ONE article: 10 glaucoma patients and 10 controls, each position held 2 minutes. Downward Dog went from 17 to 28 (glaucoma) and 17 to 29 mmHg (normal); 'The highest IOP increase (P<0.01) was measured in the Adho Mukha Svanasana position'; IOP 'dropped back to baseline values within two minutes after returning to a sitting position'; glaucoma vs normal P = 0.813. Glaucoma group median age 62, controls 36. Opened the Baskaran abstract on Europe PMC: 75 subjects from a yoga training institute; mean rise 15.1 mmHg on entering headstand and 15.8 at 5 minutes, 'twice the baseline'; no correlation with age; 'maintained during the posture in all age groups'. Opened NCCIH page (last updated August 2023): 'Older adults may need to be particularly cautious'; beginners should avoid headstands and shoulder stands; severe high blood pressure, balance issues and glaucoma may need modifications. Cramer 2013 abstract (authors are Cramer, Krucoff, Dobos): 'patients with glaucoma should avoid inversions'. Corrections: (1) original line 'The flag is conditions like glaucoma, not age' overstates; NCCIH still flags older adults, so the story now ends on the eye doctor instead. (2) The draft 'fit' claimed Downward Dog raised pressure more than the feared inversions; that is only true against Halasana and legs up the wall inside the 2015 study. Headstand was not tested there, and the 2006 headstand rise (about 15 mmHg) is larger than the 2015 Downward Dog rise (11 to 12 mmHg). Do not compare across the two studies.
kept.safety: Passes if framed as 'age alone did not predict the eye-pressure rise', never as 'inversions are safe for everyone over 50'. Put on screen: 'Glaucoma or high blood pressure? Ask your eye doctor first.' No health claim beyond the study numbers. No war, royalty, religion or lineage content.
kept.joke_angle: Boonchu has called Downward Dog his 'resting' position for 20 years. In the 2015 study it raised eye pressure more than Plow. So his eyes have been doing a harder practice than he has.

kept.title: Six months upside down, goodbye grey hair
kept.story: An old yoga text, the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, teaches Viparita Karani: head on the ground, feet to the sky, 'for a second only the first day, and increase this time daily.' Then it promises: 'After six months, the wrinkles and grey hair are not seen.' The first line is great coaching. We found no study that tests the second.
kept.asana: Viparita Karani (a mudra in the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, not an Ashtanga series asana); nearest in Ashtanga: Sarvangasana and Sirsasana in the finishing sequence
kept.source: Svatmarama, Hatha Yoga Pradipika, chapter 3, verses 80-81, translated by Pancham Sinh (Allahabad: Panini Office, 1914; the scanned copy is dated 1915).
kept.evidence: sacred-texts.com blocked automated access (Cloudflare), so I opened the scanned Pancham Sinh translation on archive.org (Central Secretariat Library copy, 'The Hatha yoga pradipika', Sinh, Allahabad). Chapter 3, verse 80 reads: 'Place the head on the ground and the feet up into the sky, for a second only the first day, and increase this time daily.' Verse 81: 'After six months, the wrinkles and grey hair are not seen. He who practises it daily, even for two hours, conquers death.' Verses 78-79 name it 'The Viparita Karani' and say it is learnt from the guru. Verse 29 confirms Maha Vedha 'destroys old age, grey hair, and shaking of the body'. Both quotes in the story are exact. The 'conquers death' clause is left out on purpose. Note: the Jasien 2015 'Viparita Karani' (lowest rise, 17 to 21 mmHg) was legs up the wall, a different shape from the text's head-on-ground practice, so do not attach those numbers to this verse. My web search budget ran out, so I could not re-check the 'no study' line myself; it is worded as a hedge ('we found no study').
kept.safety: Respectful: quotes the text exactly, praises its first instruction, and makes no fun of the text, Svatmarama or tradition. No promise of anti-ageing results. The death/immortality clause is left out. No war, royalty or religious conflict.
kept.joke_angle: Boonchu has gone upside down most mornings for 20 years and is still waiting for month six. Use only if his hair really is grey; the joke is on his hair, never on the text.

kept.title: In headstand, the head just rests
kept.story: Myth: in headstand, the arms do the work and the head just rests. A 2015 study measured 45 practitioners aged 18 to 60: at peak moments the head carried 40 to 48% of body weight. Lifting up with straight legs together tended to mean lower, slower loading and a more neutral neck than bent-leg entries.
kept.asana: Sirsasana (finishing sequence); the Intermediate Series also ends with seven headstands (Baddha Hasta Sirsasana A to D, Mukta Hasta Sirsasana A to C)
kept.source: Hector R, Jensen JL. 'Sirsasana (headstand) technique alters head/neck loading: Considerations for safety.' Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies 2015;19(3):434-441. doi:10.1016/j.jbmt.2014.10.002 (PMID 26118514).
kept.evidence: PubMed blocked automated access, so I read the same abstract on Europe PMC (PMID 26118514). It says: 'Three matched groups of 15 each (18-60 years old)'; 'All 45 practitioners performed 3 headstands'; straight legs together 'trended towards the lowest loads' (Cohen's d = 0.53 and 0.39) and 'produced slower loading rates and more neutral cervical conditions'; 'Subjects loaded the head with maximums of 40-48% of total body weight.' Fixes: 'filmed' changed to 'measured' (kinematics and force data, not just video); 'experienced' removed because the abstract says only 'practitioners'. A secondary summary says each group was 2 men and 13 women with an active headstand practice, but I could not open the full text to confirm. The note's quote about cervical risk 'especially in women and aging individuals' is NOT in the PubMed abstract; secondary sources put it in the thesis version, so do not quote it. The '50% at risk' figure stays out. The Intermediate headstand list matches the repo's own series data (ashtanga-graph.js) and the standard series.
kept.safety: No overstated claim: the study says the straight-leg entry 'may reduce' load, and the story says 'tended to'. It does not say headstand is dangerous or safe for everyone. No war, royalty, religion or lineage content.
kept.joke_angle: Boonchu's head carries almost half his body weight every morning, which is more heavy lifting than it does for the rest of the day.

kept.title: Yoga is gentle, so it can't hurt
kept.story: Myth: yoga is too gentle to hurt anyone. US emergency rooms saw an estimated 29,590 yoga injuries from 2001 to 2014, most often to the trunk. In 2014 the rate for ages 65 and over was 57.9 per 100,000 practitioners, against 11.9 for ages 18 to 44. A review of 94 trials found yoga as safe as other exercise.
kept.asana: No single asana; the trunk was the most injured region (46.6%). Ashtanga survey (Mikkonen 2008): hamstring, knee and low back were the most common sites, with no asana named in the abstract.
kept.source: Swain TA, McGwin G. 'Yoga-Related Injuries in the United States From 2001 to 2014.' Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine 2016;4(11):2325967116671703. Cramer H, Ward L, Saper R, Fishbein D, Dobos G, Lauche R. 'The Safety of Yoga: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.' American Journal of Epidemiology 2015;182(4):281-293. Optional: Mikkonen J, Pedersen P, McCarthy PW. International Journal of Yoga Therapy 2008;18(1):59-64.
kept.evidence: Opened PMC5117171: '29,590 yoga-related injuries seen in hospital emergency departments from 2001 to 2014'; 2014 rates per 100,000 participants were 65+ 57.9, 45-64 17.7, 18-44 11.9; 'The trunk (46.6%) was the most frequent region injured'; 'sprain/strain (45.0%) accounted for the majority of diagnoses'. Fix: the draft line 'Most were trunk sprains and strains' merged two separate figures (region and diagnosis), and neither is over 50%, so it now reads 'most often to the trunk'. Opened the Cramer 2015 abstract on Europe PMC: of 301 trials, '94 (1975-2014; total of 8,430 participants) reported on adverse events'; 'yoga appears as safe as usual care and exercise'. Mikkonen 2008 (University of South Wales abstract page): 110 respondents (37% response), 62% had an injury lasting over a month, 1.18 new injuries per 1,000 hours, top sites hamstring, knee and low back. The sample was self-selected, so do not present it as a population rate.
kept.safety: Factual and not alarmist. The story ends on the trials review so it does not scare older viewers away. Emergency-room data miss injuries treated elsewhere. If the Ashtanga survey is used, present it without blaming the method or the lineage. Cramer 2013 mentions one death case; it is not used. No war, royalty or religion.
kept.joke_angle: At 53, Boonchu is in the 45 to 64 group (17.7 per 100,000). His plan is to stay in this group as long as possible, and to enter the next one very slowly, after a long warm-up for his stiff hamstrings.

kept.title: Yoga either fixes pain or causes it
kept.story: Myth: yoga either fixes pain or causes it. A one-year study of 354 people from two yoga studios found both. 10.7% got new pain from yoga, mostly in the shoulder, elbow, wrist and hand. 21% of existing injuries got worse. Yet 74% said yoga improved pain they already had. Researchers say the risk may be similar to other sports.
kept.asana: Adho Mukha Svanasana (Downward Dog), named by the researchers as an example of postures that put weight on the arms; Chaturanga Dandasana is a similar arm-loading posture (not named in the study). Both are in Surya Namaskara A and B, the start of every Ashtanga series.
kept.source: Campo M, Shiyko MP, Kean MB, Roberts L, Pappas E. 'Musculoskeletal pain associated with recreational yoga participation: A prospective cohort study with 1-year follow-up.' Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies 2018;22(2):418-423. doi:10.1016/j.jbmt.2017.05.022 (PMID 29861244). Worsened/improved figures and the downward dog remark: University of Sydney news release, 28 June 2017 (Assoc. Prof. Evangelos Pappas).
kept.evidence: Abstract (fetched from the Europe PMC record for PMID 29861244; the PubMed page itself only showed a cookie wall): 'The final sample included 354 participants from two suburban yoga studios. The incidence rate of pain caused by yoga was 10.7%. More than one-third of incident cases resulted in lost yoga participation time and/or symptoms lasting more than 3 months.' The authors, journal, volume, pages and DOI all match. The Sydney release says '21 per cent of existing injuries made worse' and '74 per cent of participants in the study reported that existing pain was improved by yoga'. New pain was mostly in the upper extremities (shoulder, elbow, wrist, hand), possibly from 'downward dog and similar postures that put weight on the upper limbs'. The incidence 'may be comparable to the rates of other sports'. FIX: the original said '74% of people with existing pain'. The release says '74 per cent of participants', so I reworded it to '74% said yoga improved pain they already had'. I added 'hand' to the body parts and added the line comparing the risk to other sports. Asana check: the ashtangayoga.info Surya Namaskara A page lists Chaturanga Dandasana and Adho-Mukha-Shvanasana in the sequence.
kept.safety: No violence, politics or religion. Pain improvement is self-reported, so keep the word 'said' and do not claim yoga cures pain. The sample came from only two suburban studios. Do not invent or imply injuries Boonchu has not confirmed. A natural tie-in is the researchers' own advice: tell your teacher about injuries before class.
kept.joke_angle: Boonchu counts himself in the 74%: twenty years of daily practice have moved his hamstrings from 'concrete' to 'slightly softer concrete'.

kept.title: A hot room sweats out toxins
kept.story: Myth: a hot, sweaty practice flushes out toxins. Physiologist Pascal Imbeault's team estimated that two litres of sweat carry less than one-tenth of a nanogram of fat-stored pollutants: about 0.02% of what we take in from food each day. Kidneys and liver do the cleaning. An old text, the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, says to rub sweat in to make the body strong.
kept.asana: Surya Namaskara A and B (the heat-building start of every Ashtanga series), and the whole practice in a warm Bangkok room. In Ashtanga, heat is meant to come from breath and movement, not from a heated room.
kept.source: Imbeault P, Ravanelli N, Chevrier J. 'Can POPs be substantially popped out through sweat?' Environment International 2018;111:131-132. doi:10.1016/j.envint.2017.11.023 (PMID 29197670). Figures as reported in Erika Engelhaupt, 'Can you really sweat out toxins?', National Geographic, first published 6 April 2018 (updated 7 August 2023). Hatha Yoga Pradipika 2.13, tr. Pancham Sinh (Panini Office, 1914; some catalogues say 1915).
kept.evidence: National Geographic (Engelhaupt): Imbeault is an 'exercise physiologist at the University of Ottawa' who studies 'the pollutants stored in body fat' ('persistent organic pollutants... pesticides, flame retardants, and polychlorinated biphenyls'). A typical person doing '45 minutes of high-intensity exercise could sweat a total of two liters in a day' and 'all that sweat would contain less than one-tenth of a nanogram of these pollutants'. 'The amount in sweat is .02 percent of what you ingest every day on a typical diet.' 'That's what our kidneys and liver are for.' The article also says sweat is 'more than 99 percent water' and that small amounts of lead and BPA do get into sweat. Europe PMC confirms the Imbeault citation, volume, pages and DOI. HYP 2.13: sacred-texts.com returned 403, so I checked a scanned copy of the Pancham Sinh translation already on disk (an Internet Archive scan): 'The perspiration exuding from exertion of practice should be rubbed into the body (and not wiped), as by so doing the body becomes strong. 13.' Context: verses 2.11-2.13 are about breath-retention (kumbhaka) practice. I changed only the wording: '0.02% of daily dietary intake' became 'of what we take in from food', and I dropped 'not detox' because the verse gives strength as its reason and never mentions detox.
kept.safety: No violence, politics or mockery. The story refers only to fat-stored pollutants, so it stays accurate. Do not say sweat contains 'nothing', because trace metals and BPA do appear in it. Present the HYP line as what the old text says, not as a health claim. NCCIH (Aug 2023) warns that 'hot yoga has special risks related to overheating and dehydration'. Worth a hydration reminder in the caption. The Bikram temperature study was not used (it was sponsor-run).
kept.joke_angle: Bangkok gives Boonchu free hot yoga at 5 a.m. every day; after twenty years, the only thing he has detoxed is his towel budget.

kept.title: Twists wring toxins out of your organs
kept.story: Myth: twists wring toxins out of your organs like a wet towel. Herpreet Thind, a UMass Lowell researcher on yoga and chronic disease, told Yoga Journal there is 'no scientific basis' for this. A healthy liver cleans the body without twisting. Thind says twists still help flexibility, but we don't know what they do to the organs.
kept.asana: Marichyasana C and D (Primary Series); Ardha Matsyendrasana (Intermediate Series). Pasasana and Bharadvajasana are other Intermediate twists if needed.
kept.source: Shawn Radcliffe, 'Does Yoga Really "Detox" Your Body?', Yoga Journal, 18 January 2022 (quotes Herpreet Thind, PhD, MPH, University of Massachusetts Lowell).
kept.evidence: I downloaded the Yoga Journal page directly. Its metadata gives the byline Shawn Radcliffe and datePublished 2022-01-18. Article text: 'The short answer: We don't know.' Thind is quoted: 'Sometimes yoga instructors mention that twists [...] might be helpful [for detoxification], but there's no scientific basis for that.' She is 'a researcher at UMass Lowell who studies the benefits of physical activity and yoga for chronic disease prevention and treatment'. On the liver: 'When healthy, the liver is very efficient at detoxifying the body. It can do this work even without the benefit of twists, forward folds, or excess heat.' Thind says twists have some benefits, meaning 'the enhanced muscle flexibility that comes with regular practice', and adds: 'We don't know whether twisting or inversions are actually stimulating our internal organs.' Asana check: the ashtangayoga.info Primary Series sheet lists Maricyasana A B C D, and the Intermediate (Nadi Shodhana) sheet lists Ardha Matsyendrasana after Bharadvajasana. The original story was accurate. I only simplified the wording and made 'we don't know' explicit, so the story does not claim twists are proven useless.
kept.safety: Source tier is a magazine quoting a researcher, not a study, so phrase it as 'no evidence', not 'proven false'. The article credits the 'squeeze-and-soak' idea to B.K.S. Iyengar. Do not name him or frame it as a teacher being wrong. Make no claim either way about organ stimulation. No violence, politics or religion. This pairs well with the sweat item as a two-part detox Reel.
kept.joke_angle: Boonchu has twisted into Marichyasana D every morning for twenty years; if twists wrung out toxins he would be the cleanest man in Bangkok. Instead he is just the stiffest.

kept.title: You need a spiritual reason to start yoga
kept.story: Myth: you need a spiritual reason to start yoga. In a 2012 survey of 2,567 Australian yoga students, about 71% started for health and fitness. Only 19% first saw yoga as a spiritual practice; once practicing, 43% did. The US health agency NCCIH says yoga is rooted in Indian philosophy and began as a spiritual practice.
kept.asana: None. Neither source names an asana; do not attach one.
kept.source: NCCIH, 'Yoga: What You Need To Know' (last updated August 2023). Penman S, Cohen M, Stevens P, Jackson S. 'Yoga in Australia: Results of a national survey.' International Journal of Yoga 2012;5(2):92-101. doi:10.4103/0973-6131.98217 (PMC3410203).
kept.evidence: NCCIH page ('Last Updated: August 2023'): 'Yoga is an ancient and complex practice, rooted in Indian philosophy. It began as a spiritual practice but has become popular as a way of promoting physical and mental well-being.' Penman 2012 (PMC full text): 3,892 completed the survey, leaving '2,567 yoga practitioner respondents' after excluding teachers and overseas respondents. 'The typical yoga survey respondent was a 41-year-old, tertiary educated, employed, health-conscious female (85% women).' On reasons: 'Health and fitness', and 'increased flexibility/muscle tone' were the most common reasons for starting (both about 71%). 'Only 19% of students initially saw yoga as a spiritual practice; however, this increased to 43% once practicing.' Personal development rose from 29% to 59%. People 'often continued practicing for stress management'. FIX: neither source says anything about 'joining a religion', so that myth cannot be confirmed from these sources. I reframed the myth around spiritual motive, which the survey measures directly. I also corrected 'most started for muscle tone and flexibility': health and fitness tied with flexibility at about 71%.
kept.safety: Most sensitive item. I removed the word 'religion' because the sources do not address it and it invites faith arguments. Keep any joke away from faith, the tradition and spirituality. Do not use the survey's religious-affiliation table, court cases or politics. Note the limits: the survey was self-selected, 85% women, and Australian only. If Boonchu wants the original 'religion' framing, treat this item as drop.
kept.joke_angle: Boonchu admits he came to yoga twenty years ago for his hamstrings. He found calm, discipline and a 4 a.m. alarm clock; the hamstrings are still on their way.
